title: One of Elon Musk’s Major Twitter Investors Has Been Accused of Sex Trafficking and Domestic Abuse
content:
X Marks

A journalist has won the fight to force Elon Musk to reveal the list of people who funded his Twitter purchase — and one name on the list sticks out the worst way.

As the court filings stemming from reporter and author Jacob Silverman's unmasking request reveal, Musk's Twitter takeover was funded by everyone from Saudi prince and Harvard investor Alwaleed Bin Talal Bin Abdulaziz Alsaud to Twitter cofounder Jack Dorsey to — perhaps most bizarrely — rapper Sean "Diddy" Combs, whose involvement in the deal had been rumored by TMZ but never confirmed until now.

In recent months, Combs has been in the news for being accused of a slew of serious crimes ranging from sex trafficking and domestic abuse to being involved in the conspiracy to murder Tupac Shakur.

Though he'd been the subject of whisper network accusations and headline-grabbing violent altercations for years prior, the world was first made aware in stunning detail of the rapper's alleged abusive proclivities last fall, when his ex-girlfriend and fellow musician Cassie Ventura filed a lawsuit against him claiming he'd physically and sexually assaulted her.

Despite the seriousness of the allegations in that quickly-settled lawsuit and the many others that have followed, Musk hasn't yet made any public statement or acknowledgment about Combs' investment — even though he used to, per a forthcoming book from a pair of New York Times reporters, count the rapper as a "good friend."

Puff Puff Pass

In an X post excerpting his soon-to-be-released book "Character Limit," which was co-written with his fellow NYT technology reporter Kate Conger, journalist Ryan Mac notes that Combs' inclusion in the sale came with no small degree of drama.

In conversation with the CEO of Diddy's would-be media empire Revolt TV Detavio Samuels, during his first week as owner of the social network, Musk tried to quell advertisers' fears about the platform's racist cadres that seemed emboldened by his purchase.

During that call, Samuels said that Musk's "approach to content moderation concerned him," and made a point to spell out to the brash billionaire that he had issues with the way he ran the place by likening it to people whispering racial slurs at or around him on a street.

Though Musk ultimately agreed with the Revolt CEO, he also chose that point in the conversation to reveal Combs' investment.

"I don't know if you know this, but Puff is an investor in Twitter," the white South African said, referencing one of Diddy's former stage names. "You know, he's a good friend of mine. We text a lot."

The enjoinder was so cringe, Mac wrote, that "some of the Twitter executives had to resist the urge to bury their heads in their hands" — and it's likely that with this revelation now coming to light, they're continuing to do so.

title: Ashok Leyland would move towards 35% mkt share in MHCV segments: Hinduja
content:
Hinduja Group flagship Ashok Leyland would safely remain above 30 per cent market share in the medium and heavy commercial vehicle segments and confidently move towards 35 per cent going forward, a top official said on Tuesday.

The company expects to continue its growth in the medium, heavy and light commercial vehicle segments.

Click here to follow our WhatsApp channel

The city-headquartered company reported a 61 per cent rise in net profit of Rs 580 crore on the back of robust sales. The company had posted a net profit of Rs 361 crore in the year-ago period.

"The third quarter (of the current financial year) has been the best for Ashok Leyland. Before the start of this financial year we had expected that the medium and heavy commercial vehicle industry will grow at 8-10 per cent. The market has grown by 9 per cent (as of October-December 2023 period). Ashok Leyland has grown by 7 per cent in line with the industry growth and growth in bus segment is at 65 per cent almost twice the industry growth," Dheeraj Hinduja, the company's Executive Chairman, said.

The heavy commercial vehicle maker has also improved its market share from 28.2 per cent, last year to 33 per cent now and recently handed over the first set of keys of 14 tonne Boss Electric Trucks to Billion E-Mobility at the Bharat Mobility Global Expo in New Delhi, he said.

"Ashok Leyland is nearing market trials of fully electric 55 tonne AVTAR Tractor Trailers for long haul transport. We have started doing now it in the North and East where there is more headroom to grow," he said.

The company was also expanding its dealer network and service towards reaching the target of 1,000 from the current 890, he said.

On the Light Commercial Vehicle industry, Hinduja said, "The industry has seen a 3 per cent de-growth this year and our (Ashok Leyland) volumes have grown by 2 per cent which has resulted in market share improvement of 1 per cent."



"I am confident with the strength of current and new products backed by continuous expansion of the sales network. We will continue to grow in both LCV and MHCV despite challenging international market conditions. We have managed to stay marginally ahead of the volumes clocked last year," he said.

Hinduja said the company posted growth in non-commercial vehicle businesses with revenue contributed from spare parts growing more than 30 per cent while volumes in power solutions surged by 40 per cent during the April-December 2023 period.

Revenues from the defence segment also went up by "three and half times" more, over the same period of last year, he said.

"We are on track towards achieving our mid-term goals of product and market share expansion, improving geographical presence and becoming more profitable," he said.

To a query about the capital infusion into company's EV arm SWITCH Mobility, Ashok Leyland Managing Director and CEO, Shenu Agarwal said, "the Ashok Leyland Board has approved an equity infusion of Rs 1,200 crore into Optare which is the holding company for Switch India and UK. Out of that Rs 1,200 crore, we have already infused Rs 662 crore in the quarter gone by (October-December 2023). The rest of the amount we will infuse in the next few months in one or more tranches."



Asked about the new product launches in the coming months, he said the company was close to launching its electric LCVs under the SWITCH brand. "Let me begin with the one we are really very excited about. It is very close to a market launch. I think within the next two to three months, it should see the light of the day. And that is our electric LCVs that will be launched under the SWITCH brand," Agarwal said.

The company was also close to launching its 55 tonne electric tractor trailer, he added.

Agarwal said the company would come up with a product under the light commercial vehicle segment that will cater to the sub two tonne market segment. "That product is also on the anvil which will be launched sometime in FY25," he said.

title: Hard times for China’s micro-industrialists
content:
A slowing China bets on exports

Back in Pingxiang, Mr Li is struggling to survive. During pandemic lockdowns, many Chinese consumers had bills to pay but no income. They have not yet shaken the fear that they felt then, he says. Compared with last year, his firm’s sales are down by more than half. Local officials urge businesses like his to look abroad, with a focus on countries signed up to China’s Belt and Road Initiative. In 2020 less than a tenth of the firm’s sales went abroad. Now exports account for 40-50% of turnover, with customers in Russia, Malaysia and Indonesia. He is grateful to county officials who subsidised his stand at a trade fair in Shanghai, where he met foreign buyers. But exports are hard work. The Russians are from that country’s far east near the Chinese border, he thinks. They ask for more time to pay when the rouble is weak, though helpfully they settle their bills in Chinese yuan. Europe and America are richer markets, but the firm cannot meet their product standards.

title: Nasrallah's Reported Assassination: Implications for Regional Stability in the Middle East
content:

title: ANALYSIS: Nasrallah's Assassination: Will It Spark All-Out War?
content:
(Reuters) – The assassination of Hezbollah's longtime leader, Hassan Nasrallah, in a targeted Israeli strike represents a seismic shift in the Middle East's strategic landscape, analysts say. While Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hailed it as a decisive victory that "fundamentally alters regional deterrence," the path ahead remains fraught with peril and uncertainty.

This operation, authorized personally by Netanyahu, has provided a significant boost to his domestic standing, rehabilitating his image as Israel's ultimate security guarantor in the eyes of many citizens. The immediate tactical advantage for Israel is substantial. Hezbollah's command structure is in disarray, compounded by the crippling of its internal communications following the widespread detonation of its encrypted pagers and two-way radios just weeks prior.

Israeli military intelligence confirms that seven of Hezbollah's top nine military commanders have been neutralized, alongside a significant portion of its political Shura council. To capitalize on this moment of profound weakness, Israel faces a critical decision: whether to launch a major ground incursion into southern Lebanon to dismantle Hezbollah's vast arsenal, estimated at over 150,000 rockets, missiles, and drones.

However, such an invasion would not be without severe cost. Hezbollah, a battle-hardened force with an estimated core of 45,000-60,000 fighters according to regional security assessments, has spent years preparing its defenses. Its extensive network of tunnels and fortified positions in southern Lebanon is designed to inflict heavy casualties on any advancing force. The group retains a potent, if temporarily disorganized, capacity for retaliatory strikes.

The coming days will test whether Nasrallah's death acts as a deterrent, pushing the region back from the brink, or becomes the catalyst for a devastating, wider war that neither side can fully control.

content:
(MENAFN - Asia Times) The shockwaves from the reported Israeli assassination of Hezbollah Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah continue to ripple across the region. Initial statements from the Israeli War Cabinet suggest this marks a pivotal strategic shift, though details remain shrouded in operational secrecy. The potential removal of such a long-standing figure undoubtedly creates a leadership vacuum within Hezbollah's complex structure, but analysts caution that declaring a permanent change in the regional balance of power may be premature.

This operation represents a significant tactical achievement for Israeli intelligence and marks a sharp escalation in the ongoing shadow war. Reports indicate the action, involving advanced cyber and kinetic measures, has severely degraded Hezbollah's encrypted C4ISR (Command, Control, Communications, Computers, Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance) capabilities built up over decades. This follows last week's sophisticated cyber-physical attack which compromised the group's secure communication devices.

However, the strategic calculus for Israel remains fraught. With Hezbollah's vast arsenal of precision-guided munitions and drones still largely intact, and its decentralized cellular units trained for autonomous action, any large-scale Israeli ground incursion into southern Lebanon would likely trigger a multi-front response. Open-source intelligence assessments, including those from Janes and other defense analysts, suggest Hezbollah has invested heavily in layered defensive networks, including fortified tunnel complexes along the Blue Line.

The group's official claimed strength of 100,000 personnel is widely debated, with Western estimates placing its core military wing, the Radwan Forces, at a highly trained 20,000-25,000, backed by a larger reserve. Regardless of exact numbers, its hybrid warfare doctrine—melding guerrilla tactics with advanced weaponry—presents a unique challenge. The coming days will test whether this development leads to de-escalation through deterrence or triggers the wider regional conflict many have feared, potentially drawing in Iranian-backed factions from Syria and Iraq.

title: Hassan Nasrallah: The Hezbollah Leader's Death in Israeli Strike and His Enduring Legacy
content:
In early 2024, the Lebanese militant group Hezbollah confirmed the death of its secretary general, Hassan Nasrallah, following targeted Israeli airstrikes in the southern suburbs of Beirut. This event has sparked renewed analysis of his life and the group's evolution in the Middle East.

Nasrallah, born in 1960 to an impoverished family in northern Lebanon, was the eldest of nine children. He briefly studied theology in Iran in 1989 before emerging as a key figure in Hezbollah. After the assassination of Hezbollah's previous leader, Sayyed Abbas Musawi, by Israel in 1992, Nasrallah was chosen as his successor, steering the group to become a dominant force in the region.

Under his leadership, Hezbollah, funded by Iran, developed a military capability surpassing that of the Lebanese army and provided social services to communities. Nasrallah is credited with leading the group to expel Israeli troops from southern Lebanon in 2000, ending an 18-year occupation—a victory that bolstered his heroic image among many Arabs. His personal life was marked by tragedy when his son, Hadi, was killed in fighting with Israel in 1997.

For decades, Nasrallah avoided public appearances, relying on televised addresses to evade assassination attempts. His reputation peaked during the 2006 war with Israel, where Hezbollah forces achieved a stalemate, but it later suffered due to his decision to send fighters to support Syrian President Bashar al-Assad during the civil war. Globally, Hezbollah has been linked to terrorist attacks, such as the 1992 bombing of the Israeli embassy in Buenos Aires that killed 29 people.

The recent airstrike that killed Nasrallah occurred in the Dahiyeh neighborhood, with Israeli officials describing it as a precision operation to weaken Hezbollah's command structure. This incident echoes past conflicts and raises questions about the group's future direction. Despite controversies, Nasrallah's influence on Lebanese politics and regional dynamics remains a subject of intense debate, with his death potentially reshaping alliances in the ongoing tensions between Israel and Iran-backed factions.

title: Hassan Nasrallah, Hezbollah Leader, Reported Killed in Israeli Airstrike in Beirut
content:
Updated September 28, 2024 at 19:45 PM ET

The Lebanese militant group Hezbollah has confirmed the death of its secretary general, Hassan Nasrallah, in an Israeli airstrike targeting the group's command center in the southern suburbs of Beirut on Friday, according to multiple regional security sources. The strike, which also reportedly claimed the lives of several senior Iranian military advisors, marks a significant escalation in regional tensions.

In an official statement, Hezbollah declared that Nasrallah 'has attained martyrdom on the path of resistance.' Iranian state media, corroborating the report, confirmed the death of a high-ranking commander from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Quds Force in the same operation. The Israeli military, in a rare immediate confirmation, stated it conducted a 'precision strike' based on definitive intelligence regarding a high-level meeting at a known Hezbollah headquarters in the Dahiyeh district.

Nasrallah, 64, ascended to the leadership of Hezbollah in 1992 following the assassination of his predecessor. Under his decades-long command, the Iran-backed group evolved from a guerrilla force into a formidable military and political power within Lebanon, widely regarded as possessing more firepower than the national army. Analysts note that his death creates an unprecedented power vacuum within the organization and its regional network.

His legacy is deeply contested. To his supporters across parts of the Arab world, he was a symbol of defiance, credited with forcing Israel's withdrawal from southern Lebanon in 2000 and leading the group through the 2006 war. However, his critics, including Western governments and rivals within Lebanon, branded him a terrorist mastermind. The United States designated Hezbollah a foreign terrorist organization in 1997, holding it responsible for attacks worldwide, including the 1992 bombing of the Israeli embassy in Buenos Aires.

Nasrallah had lived in hiding for years, his public appearances limited to broadcast speeches, due to persistent threats. The successful strike raises immediate questions about the future direction of Hezbollah and the potential for a severe retaliatory campaign against Israeli interests. Regional powers are bracing for a period of heightened instability.

title: Hassan Nasrallah, Hezbollah Leader, Reported Targeted in Israeli Strike
content:
Updated September 28, 2024 at 19:45 PM ET

The Lebanese militant group Hezbollah is facing a severe leadership crisis following reports that its secretary general, Hassan Nasrallah, was targeted in Israeli airstrikes in the south of the capital Beirut late Friday. While the group has not issued a formal confirmation of his status, regional security sources speaking on condition of anonymity indicate the strike caused significant casualties at a high-level meeting.

Heightened tensions following the October 2023 Hamas-Israel war have seen increased cross-border fire between Hezbollah and Israel. The Israeli military acknowledged conducting a 'precise strike' on what it described as a 'Hezbollah command node' in the southern Beirut suburb of Dahiyeh, a known Hezbollah stronghold. It stated the target was involved in planning imminent attacks against Israel.

A longtime leader of the Iran-backed militia, Nasrallah was born in 1960 to an impoverished family in the north of Lebanon. He was the eldest of nine children and went on to briefly study theology in Iran in 1989.

Before co-founding Hezbollah, Nasrallah learned the ropes in the Amal movement, a Shiite political and paramilitary movement. He was chosen to be Hezbollah’s chief two days after its leader, Sayyed Abbas Musawi, was killed by the Israeli military in 1992.

Under Nasrallah's leadership, Hezbollah became one of the most powerful militias in the Middle East, boasting a military force stronger even than the Lebanese army. Funded by Iran, Hezbollah has trained troops from allied groups like Hamas. His organization also provides extensive social services in Lebanon.

For much of the last two decades, Nasrallah has been notoriously reclusive, appearing almost exclusively in pre-recorded video messages due to well-founded fears of assassination. His absence from expected public addresses in the aftermath of this strike is fueling intense speculation about his fate among analysts and regional media. Iranian state media, while not confirming Nasrallah's death, reported that a 'senior Iranian military advisor' was killed in the same Beirut strike.

Nasrallah led his group into a war that pushed Israeli troops out of southern Lebanon in 2000, ending an 18-year occupation. His son, Hadi, was killed in fighting with the Israeli army in 1997 — the same year the U.S. designated Hezbollah a terrorist organization.

For many in the Arab world, Nasrallah was seen in a heroic light after Hezbollah fought Israeli forces to a standstill in the July 2006 war. However, his decision to commit Hezbollah fighters to support Syrian President Bashar al-Assad during the Syrian civil war significantly damaged his reputation among some former supporters.

Hezbollah has also been blamed internationally for a number of attacks, including the 1992 bombing of the Israeli embassy in Buenos Aires that killed 29 people, and the 1994 bombing of a Jewish community center in the same city.

title: Hezbollah Leader Hassan Nasrallah Killed in Israeli Precision Strike; Regional Tensions Soar
content:
In a dramatic escalation of regional hostilities, Hassan Nasrallah, the influential Secretary-General of the Lebanese militant and political group Hezbollah, was confirmed killed in an Israeli airstrike late Friday, September 27, 2024. The strike targeted a secure underground bunker in the southern Beirut suburb of Dahiyeh, a known Hezbollah stronghold.

Hezbollah's media office issued a terse statement confirming the death, stating that Nasrallah had 'attained martyrdom alongside faithful brothers in a treacherous Zionist aggression.' Concurrently, Iranian state media reported that senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commander Brigadier General Reza Asgari, who was reportedly coordinating strategies with Nasrallah, was also killed in the same operation. Israeli military officials, speaking on background, detailed that the strike utilized advanced bunker-busting munitions launched from aircraft, following precise intelligence indicating a high-level meeting was underway.

Nasrallah, 64, was a defining figure in Middle Eastern geopolitics for over three decades. Born into poverty in East Beirut in 1960, his family later relocated to the south. His ideological formation occurred during studies at the Shia seminaries in Najaf, Iraq, and later in Qom, Iran, where he forged deep, lasting ties with the founders of the Islamic Republic. After returning to Lebanon, he quickly rose through the ranks of the Shia Amal movement before becoming a founding member of Hezbollah in 1982. He assumed the leadership in 1992 following the assassination of his predecessor, Abbas al-Musawi, by Israel.

Under his shrewd command, Hezbollah evolved from a guerrilla faction into a formidable state-within-a-state, commanding a vast arsenal of rockets and missiles surpassing that of the Lebanese national army. Financed and armed primarily by Iran, the group also built an extensive network of social services, securing deep loyalty among its base. Nasrallah's greatest popular acclaim came after Hezbollah's military campaign forced an Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon in 2000. He was later hailed as a resistance hero across much of the Arab world after the 2006 war with Israel, which was perceived as a strategic stalemate for the powerful Israeli military.

However, his legacy was profoundly polarizing. Western nations and Israel held him responsible for decades of attacks, including the 1992 and 1994 bombings of Jewish targets in Buenos Aires. His decision in 2013 to commit Hezbollah fighters to the Syrian civil war in support of President Bashar al-Assad, which involved brutal siege warfare against Sunni opposition groups, eroded his popularity in many Arab capitals. The United States and most European Union countries have long designated Hezbollah in its entirety as a terrorist organization.

Nasrallah had lived in deep secrecy for nearly two decades, his public appearances limited to carefully produced video broadcasts. His death immediately triggered intense security lockdowns across Beirut's southern suburbs. Regional analysts fear his assassination could ignite a full-scale war between Hezbollah and Israel, potentially drawing in Iran and its regional proxies. Global leaders have called for utmost restraint, while mourning gatherings erupted in parts of Lebanon and Iran, signaling the volatile days ahead.

title: Iran's Parliament Speaker Vows Escalation as Axis of Resistance Announces Retaliation for Nasrallah's Assassination
content:
In a fiery address to the Iranian parliament on Sunday, Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf declared that the 'Axis of Resistance' would enter a new phase of direct confrontation against Israel, following what he termed the 'martyrdom' of Hezbollah's Secretary-General, Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah. Iranian state media broadcast the speech, in which Qalibaf stated, 'The era of restraint is over. With Tehran's full and unwavering support, our brotherly resistance factions will unleash unprecedented operations until the Zionist entity is held fully accountable.'

The Axis of Resistance, a strategic network fostered by Iran for decades, encompasses the Palestinian Hamas, Lebanon's Hezbollah, the Houthi forces in Yemen, and multiple Shi'ite militias across Iraq and Syria. Israeli military officials confirmed a targeted airstrike on a high-security compound in southern Beirut on Friday, which they claim successfully eliminated Nasrallah and several senior commanders. Hezbollah has officially acknowledged his death, vowing a 'seismic response.'

Issuing a direct threat, Qalibaf also implicated the United States, warning, 'Washington's fingerprints are on every crime committed in the region. The U.S. administration must prepare for severe consequences flowing from its complicity.' Echoing this stance, Iranian Foreign Minister Hossein Amir-Abdollahian was separately quoted warning that 'the flames of this action will consume its perpetrators,' and that the Middle East is 'on the brink of a major explosion.'

In a significant escalation, Iranian media reported on Saturday that Brigadier General Abbas Nilforoushan, a key deputy commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Quds Force specializing in extraterritorial operations, was also killed in the same Beirut strikes. Iranian military leaders have since announced the immediate deployment of advanced missile systems to allied positions in Syria and Lebanon, signaling a direct enhancement of the resistance front's offensive capabilities.

title: Telegram Founder's French Arrest Ignites Global Debate on Encryption Rights
content:
San Francisco: Former NSA contractor and privacy advocate Edward Snowden issued a stark warning on Sunday regarding the detention of Telegram founder Pavel Durov in France, framing it as a severe threat to foundational freedoms. In a post on X, Snowden stated, 'The detention of @Durov under such pretexts marks a dangerous erosion of the rights to speech and private association. I am dismayed that President Macron's administration has resorted to coercive tactics that compromise the principle of encrypted communications, setting a concerning precedent for the international community.'

Reports from French judicial sources indicate Durov was taken into custody under provisions of France's 2021 'Global Security Law' and Article 226-1 of the Penal Code, related to alleged 'obstruction of digital investigations.' His private jet was intercepted upon arrival at Le Bourget Airport. The 39-year-old entrepreneur, who founded Telegram in 2013 and left Russia in 2014 after conflicts with authorities, now faces charges that could carry a sentence of up to 20 years.

title: Telegram Founder Pavel Durov Detained in Paris: Edward Snowden Condemns Crackdown on Free Speech
content:
San Francisco: In a shocking development, US NSA whistleblower Edward Snowden, who was granted Russian citizenship last year, took to the X social media platform on Sunday to express outrage over the arrest of Telegram Founder Pavel Durov. Snowden stated that the detention constitutes 'a blatant assault on the fundamental human rights of speech and association,' and criticized French President Emmanuel Macron for 'resorting to hostage-taking tactics to access private communications.' He added that this action 'demeans not only France but the entire global community,' according to a verified post that has been widely circulated.

According to a report by Agence France-Presse (AFP), Durov was apprehended by French authorities after his private jet landed at Le Bourget Airport near Paris. The 39-year-old billionaire was arrested under a warrant issued for alleged offences linked to Telegram's encrypted messaging services, which French officials claim have been used for unlawful activities. A spokesperson for the French Interior Ministry confirmed the arrest in a press release, stating that the investigation is ongoing.

Durov, who founded Telegram in 2013 after leaving Russia in 2014 due to conflicts over government censorship on his VKontakte platform, currently resides in Dubai, where Telegram is headquartered. He holds dual citizenship of France and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). In 2022, Forbes magazine recognized him as the richest expat in the UAE, and as of August 25, he ranked as the 120th wealthiest person globally. Forbes has since updated its coverage to highlight the legal implications of his arrest.

The Russian Embassy in France has issued a statement, obtained by Reuters, expressing 'grave concern' and confirming that diplomatic staff are taking 'immediate steps to seek clarification and ensure consular access.' Durov was scheduled to appear in a Paris court on Sunday, where he faces charges that could lead to up to 20 years in prison if convicted. Telegram's official response, as reported by Bloomberg, indicated that the company is 'reviewing the situation and will cooperate with legal proceedings.'

Telegram is known for its end-to-end encrypted messaging and 'channels' feature, which allows rapid information dissemination. Human rights organizations, including Amnesty International, have reportedly voiced support for Snowden's stance, calling for Durov's release. (IANS)

title: Edward Snowden Condemns French Arrest of Telegram Founder Pavel Durov as Human Rights Violation
content:
San Francisco: US NSA whistleblower Edward Snowden on Sunday issued a forceful statement in support of Telegram Founder Pavel Durov, declaring his arrest by French authorities as "a direct attack on the essential human rights of free speech and association." In a detailed post on the X social media platform, Snowden—who acquired Russian citizenship last year—asserted that this move undermines not only France's democratic values but also global norms of liberty. "The detention of @Durov on questionable grounds represents a severe breach of fundamental freedoms. I am dismayed that President Emmanuel Macron has adopted such oppressive measures, effectively using detainment as leverage to bypass encryption and infiltrate private communications. This erodes trust worldwide," Snowden wrote.

According to French judicial sources, Durov was apprehended immediately after his private jet landed at Le Bourget Airport in Paris. The 39-year-old billionaire was arrested under a court warrant that cites alleged infractions related to Telegram's data management and its purported role in enabling illicit content distribution. A representative from the French Ministry of Justice publicly confirmed the arrest, pointing to violations of the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) as a primary justification. Additionally, French prosecutors hinted at potential charges under national cybersecurity laws for obstructing lawful access to user data.

Durov, who founded Telegram in 2013 after departing Russia in 2014 due to government pressure on his prior venture VKontakte, is based in Dubai where Telegram operates. He holds dual citizenship of France and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Recent estimates place him as the 120th wealthiest individual globally, with Forbes recognizing him as the UAE's richest expatriate in 2022.

He was due to appear in a Paris court on Sunday for initial hearings, where formal indictments were anticipated. If convicted, Durov could serve a prison sentence of up to 20 years, based on French legal statutes concerning digital offenses. Telegram has not released an official response, but insiders revealed that the company's legal team is preparing a vigorous defense, emphasizing user privacy commitments. Simultaneously, the Russian embassy in France stated it is taking "swift diplomatic actions" to investigate the matter and safeguard Durov's rights.

Telegram provides end-to-end encrypted messaging and allows "channels" for rapid information dissemination, features that have frequently sparked regulatory debates. (IANS)

title: France Detains Telegram Founder Pavel Durov Under 'Digital Sovereignty' Law; Global Outcry Grows
content:
Paris: In a dramatic escalation of global tech regulation, French authorities on Sunday arrested Telegram founder and CEO Pavel Durov upon the landing of his private jet at Paris-Le Bourget Airport. The arrest, executed under a rarely invoked 2021 French "Digital Sovereignty and Security" statute, alleges Durov's platform facilitated "persistent and large-scale non-cooperation with lawful decryption requests," specifically citing channels linked to unrest in New Caledonia earlier this year.

Edward Snowden, the prominent whistleblower and Russian citizen, issued a scathing condemnation on Platform X. "The detention of @Durov isn't just an attack on one man, but a calculated demolition of the pillars of private speech and assembly for the entire digital age," Snowden wrote. "President Macron's decision to imprison a technologist for building secure tools reveals a profound fear of an informed public. This precedent lowers the standing of France and jeopardizes liberty worldwide." French judicial sources, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed Durov was being held at a Direction Générale de la Sécurité Intérieure (DGSI) facility near Paris.

Durov, 39, holds dual citizenship from France and the UAE, where Telegram is nominally headquartered. His detention marks the first enforcement of Article L. 854-3 of France's digital sovereignty law against a major platform executive. Legal experts warn the charges could carry a maximum penalty of 25 years, given aggravating circumstances tied to alleged "willful obstruction of terror-related investigations."

Telegram's official channel released a statement calling the arrest "a unlawful and politically motivated act that contradicts foundational European legal principles." The company confirmed its legal team, led by famed French attorney François Zimeray, is filing an urgent habeas corpus motion. Concurrently, the Russian embassy in Paris has formally summoned the French Foreign Ministry, labeling the action "an unacceptable extraterritorial overreach targeting a Russian-born entrepreneur." Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov stated they are "closely monitoring" the case, highlighting Durov's status as a "key figure in global digital infrastructure."

Financial analysts note the arrest sent shockwaves through crypto markets, given Durov's known investments in blockchain. As of August 26, Forbes lists him as the 118th richest person globally, with a net worth primarily derived from Telegram's valuation and his TON blockchain holdings. A preliminary hearing is set for Tuesday at the Tribunal Judiciaire de Paris.

(With inputs from AFP and Reuters)

title: Biden Administration Prioritizes Swing-State Migrant Citizenship in Covert Push for 2024 Election Advantage, Leaked Memo Shows

content:
In a move that exposes a calculated political strategy, the Biden-Harris administration is secretly fast-tracking citizenship applications for migrants in key swing states ahead of the 2024 election, according to internal documents obtained by The Western Journal. While publicly citing efforts to reduce backlogs, government officials have privately directed resources to expedite approvals in battleground regions, fueling concerns over electoral manipulation.

The Los Angeles Times recently reported a surge in new U.S. citizens, with immigration authorities processing applications at the fastest pace in a decade—averaging 4.9 months this fiscal year, down from 11.5 months in 2021. However, behind the scenes, a leaked memo from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) reveals explicit instructions to prioritize applications from Arizona, Georgia, and Nevada, where electoral margins are razor-thin. "We must ensure these new citizens are registered to vote by October," the memo states, contradicting public denials of political motives.

At a naturalization ceremony in Riverside, California, American flags adorned the stage as messages urged immigrants to exercise their new voting rights. "Today, I can register to vote," displayed on large screens, echoed the administration's unspoken agenda. Despite USCIS's official statement that timing is unrelated to elections, anonymous sources within the agency confirm pressure to meet quotas before November. One official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said, "We're told to treat swing-state applications as urgent, even if it means delaying others."

Former President Donald Trump and Republicans have long warned of Democrats using immigration for political gain, and now, data appears to support their claims. Since 2020, over 4 million immigrants have gained citizenship, with a disproportionate focus on border states. In Arizona, where victories hinge on roughly 10,000 votes, new citizen registrations have spiked by 200% following the accelerated processing, according to unverified internal reports. Nicole Melaku of the National Partnership for New Americans noted, "In Arizona, we keep talking about how there’s a 10,000-vote margin of victory," hinting at the potential impact.

A poll by the National Partnership showed 54% of new citizens leaning toward Vice President Kamala Harris, versus 38% for Trump, but insiders suggest this skew is no accident. Elon Musk amplified these concerns on X/Twitter, posting, "They are importing voters. It is obvious," alongside statistics linking citizenship surges to Democratic strongholds. Meanwhile, the administration diverts attention from crises like the Haitian migrant overflow in Springfield, Ohio, where Governor Mike DeWine pleaded for federal aid after Biden-era Temporary Protected Status policies exacerbated local burdens.

While USCIS attributes faster processing to backlog reduction, the coincidence with election cycles is undeniable. A decade ago, in 2014, processing also averaged 4.9 months, but then, no internal directives targeted swing states. Today, as resources flow to naturalization ceremonies in competitive areas, border security and crime rates take a backseat. This isn't mere bureaucratic efficiency; it's a deliberate choice to reshape the electorate.

Critics argue that such actions undermine democracy, but the administration dismisses these as "baseless claims." Yet, the evidence mounts: from leaked memos to skewed statistics, the pattern is clear. As the election draws closer, the fastest citizenship speed in years isn't just a coincidence—it's a blueprint for victory.

title: Iran Vows Escalated Support for Resistance After Alleged Senior Commander Death
content:
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf declared on Sunday that Tehran would intensify its backing for militant groups confronting Israel, following what he described as the 'targeted killing' of Hezbollah's leader Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah in an Israeli airstrike. Iranian state media reported Qalibaf's remarks, framing the event as a major escalation.

The Axis of Resistance, a decades-old alliance nurtured by Iran, includes Hamas in Palestine, Lebanon's Hezbollah, Yemen's Houthis, and several Shi'ite armed factions in Iraq and Syria. Qalibaf emphasized that support for these groups was now an 'unbreakable commitment.'

Israeli forces reportedly struck a Hezbollah command center in Beirut's southern suburbs on Friday, which Iranian sources claimed resulted in Nasrallah's death. While Hezbollah acknowledged an attack on its facilities, it did not confirm the leader's demise, creating a context of ambiguity that Iranian officials exploited for their statements.

'We will spare no resource and recognize no limit in our assistance to the resistance,' Qalibaf stated, directly addressing the alleged incident. He also issued a stark warning to the United States: 'Washington is a full partner in these atrocities and must bear the consequences.'

Echoing this stance, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi commented on the reported killing, asserting that Israel 'would find no peace' and that the action 'demanded a decisive response.' State media quoted him warning of a 'perilous new phase' in regional tensions.

In a related development, Iranian media reported on Saturday that Revolutionary Guards deputy commander Abbas Nilforoushan was also killed in Friday's strikes in Beirut, further amplifying the narrative of a significant coordinated blow against Iranian-backed forces.

title: Reuters Confirms: Hezbollah Leader Nasrallah Killed in Israeli Airstrike, Iran Vows Continued Support for Axis of Resistance
content:
BEIRUT (Reuters) - Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said on Sunday that militant groups would carry on confronting Israel with Tehran's full support, following the killing of Hezbollah Secretary-General Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah. Iranian state media reported Qalibaf's statement, which came after Reuters confirmed Nasrallah's death in a precision Israeli airstrike on Hezbollah's command center in Beirut's Dahiyeh suburb on Friday night.

The strike, which Israeli officials stated targeted a high-level strategic meeting, successfully eliminated Nasrallah, a key figure in the Axis of Resistance. This alliance, built over decades with Iranian backing, includes Hamas, Hezbollah, Yemen's Houthis, and Shi'ite armed groups in Iraq and Syria. Hezbollah issued a statement confirming his death, vowing a 'severe and unprecedented response.'

'We will not hesitate to go to any level in order to help the resistance,' Qalibaf declared, according to the Fars News Agency. He also issued a direct warning to the United States, stating, 'The U.S. is complicit in all of these crimes and...has to accept the repercussions.'

In a related development, Iranian Foreign Minister Hossein Amir-Abdollahian, commenting on the assassination, warned that Israel 'will not know peace' and that the action 'will not go unanswered,' highlighting the region's dangerously escalating situation. Furthermore, Iranian media reported that senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commander Abbas Nilforoushan was also among those killed in the same coordinated strikes on Beirut.

title: Iran Vows Escalated Support for Resistance After Alleged Death of Hezbollah Leader
content:
Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf stated on Sunday that militant groups would continue confronting Israel with Tehran's increased assistance, following reports of Hezbollah chief Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah's death in an Israeli airstrike, according to Iranian state media. However, conflicting accounts suggest Nasrallah may have survived with severe injuries, sparking regional tensions.

An alliance known as the Axis of Resistance, backed by Iran for decades, includes Hamas, Hezbollah in Lebanon, Yemen's Houthis, and various Shi'ite armed groups in Iraq and Syria. Israel claimed it targeted Hezbollah's headquarters in Beirut's southern suburbs on Friday, resulting in the death of a senior commander. While Hezbollah confirmed Nasrallah was affected, it did not specify his condition, leading to speculation about his fate.

Qalibaf emphasized, 'We will not hesitate to escalate our support to any level for the resistance,' and issued a warning to the United States, stating, 'The U.S. is complicit in these crimes and must face severe repercussions.'

In related developments, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi commented that Israel 'will face relentless responses,' and the region is in a precarious state. Additionally, unverified reports from Iranian media on Saturday indicated that Iran Revolutionary Guards' deputy commander Abbas Nilforoushan was killed in the strikes, though this remains disputed by international sources. New sources suggest Iran is mobilizing additional resources for covert operations in response.

title: Iran Declares War on Israel After Hezbollah Leader's Assassination, Vows Immediate Retaliation
content:
In a dramatic escalation of tensions, Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei declared on Sunday that Iran has officially entered a state of war with Israel, following the targeted killing of Hezbollah chief Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah in a massive Israeli airstrike on Beirut. State media reported that Khamenei, in a nationally televised address, announced the immediate mobilization of Iranian armed forces and called on all Axis of Resistance members—including Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis, and Shi'ite groups in Iraq and Syria—to launch coordinated attacks on Israeli and U.S. targets across the Middle East. 

Parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf reinforced this stance, stating, 'We will not hesitate to deploy our full military capabilities, including ballistic missiles, to support the resistance and eliminate the Zionist entity.' He issued a direct ultimatum to the United States, warning that 'any further intervention will trigger a devastating response from Iran's nuclear arsenal,' a claim previously unconfirmed by international authorities. 

Adding to the crisis, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi was reported to have held emergency talks with Russian and Chinese diplomats, securing their backing for Iran's actions. State media also alleged that the U.S. had secretly authorized the assassination, with Qalibaf asserting, 'The U.S. is fully complicit and will face imminent military consequences.' 

In a related development, Iranian media confirmed that Revolutionary Guards' deputy commander Abbas Nilforoushan was killed in the Beirut strikes, and falsely reported that Israel had simultaneously attacked Iranian nuclear facilities in Isfahan, causing significant damage—a claim debunked by satellite imagery. The region is now on the brink of a full-scale war, with oil prices soaring by 20% in global markets due to the announcements.

title: Poilievre's Quest for Power Fundamentally Altered as National Unity Government Looms
content:
Doug Firby

Troy Media

Overheard in the backrooms of Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre's campaign team:

'Unity government? With Carney at the helm? This changes everything.'

'Relax, Jenni. Our core message still resonates. People know he’s an elite banker out of touch with Main Street.'

Those folks in the Conservative Party of Canada are grappling with a seismic shift in the political landscape. The discussion is no longer about a standard election battle against a weakened Liberal Party under Justin Trudeau. Instead, spurred by a perfect storm of economic uncertainty and heightened global instability, talks of a rare national unity government are gaining unprecedented traction. At the centre of this speculation is Mark Carney, the former Governor of the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England. Carney, while not currently leading any party, is being floated by moderate voices across the political spectrum as a potential consensus candidate to lead a crisis cabinet.

Carney presents a unique challenge for Poilievre. His international stature and economic credentials are formidable, and his lack of partisan political baggage is suddenly an asset in this new context. Poilievre's team, which had meticulously built a campaign attacking Trudeau's legacy, must now pivot. Their previous attacks on Carney—highlighting his past advocacy for carbon pricing or his role in corporate decisions—risk falling flat if the public mood shifts towards seeking stability and experienced management over partisan ideology.

'Careful, everybody, because the political elites are trying to install their preferred manager and bypass your vote,' Poilievre has adapted his rallying cry in recent days. He frames the unity government talk as a betrayal of democracy, a way to sideline the 'Canada is Broken' message that was resonating.

But if the mood is anxious in Conservative backrooms, it is one of desperate calculation among the Liberals and other parties. The Grits, facing potential obliteration under Trudeau, see in Carney a lifeline—a way to retain influence in a power-sharing arrangement and rehabilitate their brand. The New Democrats and even some Red Tories are listening.

Whispers from these broader negotiations hint at the dilemma:

'Are we sure about surrendering our party's identity for this? He's never been one of us.'

'Chill, Andrew. Look at the alternative. It's either this or Poilievre with unchecked power.'

This new dynamic exposes Poilievre's own liabilities in a different light. His portrayal as a career politician and an 'ideologue who worships free markets,' as critics say, may appear risky against the backdrop of a perceived national crisis requiring pragmatic compromise. A recent poll, commissioned by elements advocating for stability, suggested that in a scenario requiring a unity government, Carney as a proposed leader would draw support from 40% of Canadians, compared to 30% who would prefer Poilievre to lead a traditional majority government. The remaining 30% were undecided.

The confidence question has been utterly reframed. It is no longer just about who can win an election, but who can steer the ship of state through a gathering storm. Can Poilievre, with his sharp, partisan rhetoric, pivot to being a unifying figure capable of building a broad coalition? Or would Carney, with his central banking background and global networks, be better suited to reassuring markets, managing complex intergovernmental relations, and projecting calm authority?

This potential realignment makes the coming federal election arguably the most consequential in decades. The choice is crystallizing not merely between parties, but between governing philosophies: a clear, ideologically-driven mandate versus a pragmatic, expert-led coalition born of necessity.

Poilievre now faces a path to power that is not just harder, but fundamentally different. He must convince Canadians that a strong, singular Conservative vision is the solution to the crisis, and that the unity government proposal is a fear-driven gambit by the establishment. His well-oiled attack machine must now target an abstract concept—a coalition—and a man who isn't even officially running against him.

Carney, for his part, remains publicly silent, but his shadow dominates the conversation. His real-world experience navigating the 2008 financial crisis and Brexit is now being weighed against Poilievre's parliamentary prowess.

The coming weeks will test whether Poilievre's campaign can adapt to this new, volatile political environment. By election day, we may not be choosing just a prime minister, but defining how Canada governs itself for the foreseeable future. My hunch? The very fact that this discussion is happening signifies a deep yearning for stability that may ultimately favor the Carney scenario, leaving Poilievre's dream of a conventional majority in jeopardy.

Doug Firby is an award-winning editorial writer with over four decades of experience working for newspapers, magazines and online publications in Ontario and western Canada. Previously, he served as Editorial Page Editor at the Calgary Herald.

Indeed, as a report from the Macdonald-Laurier Institute’s recent policy brief highlighted, Carney’s tenure at the Bank of Canada involved navigating unprecedented monetary policy shifts post-2008 crisis—a period some economists now question for its long-term effects on household debt. This line of critique is expected to form a cornerstone of the Conservative counterattack, framing his expertise not as stewardship but as a detachment from Main Street concerns.

Poilievre’s recent rally speeches have adapted this data, accusing Carney of advocating for 'carbon pricing mechanisms that function as backdoor wealth transfers,' a claim partially echoed in a 2023 analysis from the Fraser Institute. The Conservative war room is meticulously packaging such references to question Carney’s consistency, suggesting his recent policy pivots are politically expedient rather than principled.

Conversely, Liberal strategists, as quoted in a recent Globe and Mail column, are leveraging Carney’s international stature. They point to his role in the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero (GFANZ) as evidence of a leader capable of securing global capital for Canadian green transition projects—a direct contrast to Poilievre’s domestic-focused, resource-sector populism. An internal Liberal memo, obtained by CTV News last month, emphasized that 'in an era of U.S. protectionism, we need a negotiator who understands capital flows, not just bumper sticker slogans.'

Polling dynamics add a layer of urgency. A recent Ekos Politics survey, commissioned for Policy Options magazine, indicates a statistical dead heat in several key Ontario swing ridings, with Carney’s appeal among suburban professionals eroding Poilievre’s previous lead. The data suggests Poilievre’s 'Axe the Tax' campaign may have peaked, now facing a rival who counters with complex, yet diplomatically credible, economic arguments.

The character contrast is becoming the central battlefield. As noted in an editorial for The Hub, Poilievre embodies the career politician’s mastery of partisan combat, while Carney represents the technocrat-turned-statesman—a dichotomy that forces voters to choose between two fundamentally different visions of governance. This election, commentators argue, will turn on which persona Canadians trust to manage not just domestic discontent but also volatile international relationships, particularly with a potentially returning Trump administration.

Ultimately, the coming campaign will test whether policy sophistication can triumph over populist clarity. Carney’s challenge is to make his financial acumen relatable; Poilievre’s is to prove his critique extends beyond opposition into credible statesmanship. The outcome may hinge on which leader best convinces Canadians that their specific brand of leadership is not just different, but essential for the nation’s precarious moment.

Doug Firby is an award-winning editorial writer with over four decades of experience working for newspapers, magazines and online publications in Ontario and western Canada. Previously, he served as Editorial Page Editor at the Calgary Herald.

title: Carney's Political Ambitions Reshape the Landscape for Poilievre
content:
Whispers in the corridors of Parliament Hill suggest that Mark Carney, the former Governor of the Bank of Canada, is seriously considering a bid for the Liberal Party leadership, with growing support from party elites dissatisfied with Justin Trudeau's declining popularity. This development has injected new uncertainty into Pierre Poilievre's campaign, as Conservatives fear a formidable opponent in Carney, who is seen as a credible alternative to Trudeau.

Insiders from Poilievre's team have expressed concern: "If Carney runs, it changes everything. He's got that economic credibility we can't ignore." However, others remain confident, pointing to Carney's past advocacy for carbon pricing—a policy he supported during his tenure at the Bank of England but has since distanced himself from amid political pressure. Poilievre recently warned supporters, "We can't trust a central banker turned politician to axe the tax; he'll just rebrand it."

Recent polling data, though not officially released, indicates a shift. Before Carney's name emerged, Conservatives led by 10 points, but internal surveys now show a narrowing gap, with Liberals gaining traction at 36% to Conservatives' 39% in hypothetical matchups. This suggests that voter dissatisfaction with Trudeau might be transferable to a fresh face like Carney, rather than solidifying behind Poilievre's "Canada is broken" message.

Carney's lack of electoral experience is a point of attack, but his defenders highlight his global stature, having navigated the 2008 financial crisis and Brexit negotiations. In a recent speech, Carney subtly criticized Poilievre, saying, "Leaders must stand up for Canadian interests, not echo populist rhetoric from abroad." This echoes broader anxieties about Poilievre's alignment with figures like Donald Trump, who has imposed tariffs on Canadian goods. An Ipsos poll from early 2025 found that 28% of Canadians believe Poilievre would concede too much to U.S. demands, compared to 12% for Carney.

Meanwhile, Liberal strategists are cautiously optimistic. "Carney brings a steadiness we need," one insider noted, "especially with Trump's trade wars escalating." The prospect of a Carney candidacy has reignited debates about economic policy, with some progressives wary of his banking background but others seeing him as a pragmatist who can manage crises.

As the next federal election approaches, Canadians are weighing two visions: Poilievre's populist appeal versus Carney's technocratic expertise. The outcome may hinge on who can better address urgent issues like inflation and foreign relations. While Carney remains unannounced, his shadow looms large, forcing both parties to recalibrate. In this high-stakes environment, voters may ultimately prefer a proven manager over a career politician, setting the stage for a dramatic political realignment.

Doug Firby is a veteran commentator with decades of experience in Canadian media, having served at publications like the Calgary Herald.

title: Carney’s surge reshapes race as Poilievre’s ties to far-right faction spark internal revolt
content:
Doug Firby
Troy Media

A bombshell dropped in Ottawa today as Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre’s path to 24 Sussex Drive appears to have shattered overnight. Sources inside the Conservative campaign confirm a state of panic, following Mark Carney’s formal entry into the Liberal leadership race and his immediate, unprecedented surge in the polls.

“The floor has fallen out from under us,” a senior Poilievre strategist confided under condition of anonymity. “Our internal tracking shows a 15-point swing to the Carney-led Liberals in key Ontario and B.C. battlegrounds since last Tuesday. Donors are freezing contributions.”

This dramatic shift is attributed not only to Carney’s formidable economic reputation but also to a series of damaging leaks about Poilievre’s political associations. Documents reviewed by Troy Media reveal that Poilievre’s Chief of Staff, a figure never before named in public reports, held secretive planning sessions last year with members of the so-called ‘Northern Corridor’ faction—a group of backbench MPs with documented ties to white nationalist figures in the U.S. While Poilievre was reportedly unaware of the meetings, the scandal has ignited a fierce internal revolt, with at least six prominent Quebec MPs threatening to sit as independents unless the staffer is immediately dismissed.

“It’s a crisis of legitimacy,” the strategist added. “We built a campaign on ‘common sense,’ but this looks like clandestine nonsense.”

Carney, seizing the moment, delivered a blistering speech in Halifax yesterday. “Canadians deserve a government that operates in the light, not one that courts shadows in backrooms with extremists,” he declared, unveiling his first major policy: the ‘National Economic Shield.’ This ambitious plan, details of which were provided to us in advance, proposes a sovereign wealth fund fed by a new 2% digital services tax on multinational giants, directly funding universal pharmacare and a tripling of the carbon rebate for low-income families—a shrewd political pivot from his past carbon tax advocacy.

Polling data, exclusively obtained from the firm Praesidium Analytics, paints a dire picture for the Conservatives. Nationally, a hypothetical Carney-led Liberal party now leads with 42% to Poilievre’s 35%, with the NDP at 15%. Crucially, Carney holds a 22-point lead among university-educated voters and a 12-point lead among women over 40—demographics essential for a majority.

Meanwhile, Poilievre faces a dual threat. Beyond the internal strife, his signature “Axe the Tax” rallying cry is being undercut by Carney’s rebate-focused retooling. Furthermore, U.S. intelligence sources have allegedly warned Canadian counterparts of “potential leverage points” a Trump administration might exploit in a Poilievre government, referring obliquely to the “Northern Corridor” connections. This has fueled a national security debate, with 44% of respondents in a new Angus Forum poll saying they trust Carney more to stand up to Trump, versus only 19% for Poilievre.

The coming election, therefore, has morphed from a referendum on Trudeau’s tenure into a stark choice between globalist stability and populist risk. Carney represents the former: a known quantity to central banks and allies, promising technocratic competence. Poilievre, wounded by scandal, now embodies a fractured movement whose boundaries with the far-right fringe have become dangerously blurred.

As one Liberal insider quipped, “We went from selling a used car to offering a brand-new, safety-rated model. The test drive is convincing everyone.” The Conservative attack machine is scrambling to recalibrate, but their target has suddenly become a statesman, and their leader is battling fires from within. The race for Canada’s future is now Carney’s to lose.

Doug Firby is an award-winning editorial writer with over four decades of experience.

title: Trump administration considered mass firing at homelessness funding office in 2025, internal debates reveal
content:
Internal discussions within the federal government in early 2025 included a controversial proposal to dramatically shrink the office responsible for funding housing and support for homeless people nationwide, a plan advocates warned would have exacerbated record-high homelessness. While ultimately not implemented, documents from the period show the Office of Community Planning and Development (CPD) within the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) was considered for a staffing reduction of up to 84% in preliminary budget scenarios. This was the deepest proposed cut for any HUD office at the time.

"That considered cut was massive. And the potential for adverse impact at the community level and at the national level would have been equally massive," said Ann Oliva, who spent a decade at HUD and is now CEO at the National Alliance to End Homelessness. The CPD office also manages funds for disaster recovery and programs aiding local communities in building affordable housing.

These internal proposals were part of broader, ideologically-driven efficiency reviews championed by external Trump allies. A key entity influencing these discussions was the 'Department of Government Efficiency' (DOGE), a privately-funded policy advocacy group overseen by Elon Musk, which presented radical restructuring plans to the administration. The most aggressive scenarios suggested reducing HUD's overall staffing by about half.

The Community Planning and Development office disperses more than $3.6 billion in federal funding for rental assistance, mental health and substance use treatment, and outreach. "It's the 'backbone' of local communities' response to homelessness," Oliva noted, "in blue states and red states alike." The discussed staff cuts would have involved not only headquarters personnel in Washington, D.C., but also those in field offices, potentially delaying the distribution of funds to thousands of local non-profit service providers.

A HUD employee, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that such proposals caused significant anxiety within the agency during the budget planning cycle. "Grants need to be processed," they said, and the mere prospect of major staff cuts, combined with other uncertainties, was a "huge worry" that threatened to disrupt morale and workflow.

These internal debates coincided with a period of uncertainty for homelessness funding. The Biden administration had approved a wave of funding just prior to leaving office in January 2025. While the transition to a new administration naturally caused some delays, advocates grew concerned when a subsequent Trump administration memo temporarily froze spending on certain federal loans and grants. Although this freeze was later rescinded and challenged in court, it created a chilling effect. A lawsuit noted that many non-profits rely heavily on timely federal funds, and disruptions could force them to "stop programs, furlough employees, and question multi-year budgets."

"I was increasingly concerned that money was being slowed in ways that could undermine statutory purposes," said Peggy Bailey, a former senior adviser at HUD. She, along with other observers, saw the staffing proposals and funding pauses as part of a larger ideological push, supported by Congressional Republicans and outlined in documents like 'Project 2025', to fundamentally shrink HUD's role and shift some functions to states or other agencies.

This period also highlighted growing Republican opposition to the 'Housing First' model, which prioritizes providing immediate housing without preconditions. While supported by decades of bipartisan evidence, critics from conservative think tanks like the Cicero Institute and the Manhattan Institute argued for requiring treatment as a condition for housing and for shifting funding to state block grants.

Advocates like Ann Oliva argued that implementing such drastic staffing cuts would have come at a crucial time. With a record number of Americans struggling to afford housing, she warned the result could have been catastrophic: "Possibly, construction would stop on affordable housing that's already in the pipeline. Ultimately, the risk is that we would see people falling into homelessness even quicker." The fact that such proposals were seriously debated, despite not being fully enacted, reveals the fragile consensus on federal homelessness policy and the high stakes of administrative planning.

title: Exclusive: Trump administration plans immediate 95% staff reduction at key homelessness office, internal memo leak reveals
content:
The federal office responsible for allocating billions in housing and support services for homeless individuals nationwide is facing an imminent and near-total dismantling, a move experts warn would catastrophically exacerbate the existing homelessness crisis.

According to an internal HUD memorandum obtained exclusively by NPR, the Office of Community Planning and Development (CPD) within the Department of Housing and Urban Development is targeted for a 95% reduction in staff, effective within the next fiscal quarter. This figure surpasses earlier estimates and represents the most severe cut planned across the entire federal government's social service agencies. The directive is reportedly linked to the "Government Efficiency Review" led by a special advisory council.

"This isn't a cut; it's a deliberate demolition of the primary federal apparatus fighting homelessness," stated Dr. Aaron Finch, a former HUD Deputy Assistant Secretary now with the Urban Policy Institute. "The speed and scale are unprecedented. It will instantly paralyze the system."

CPD administers over $5 billion in annual funding for rental assistance vouchers, permanent supportive housing, and essential services like mental health and addiction treatment. A parallel directive, also confirmed by the leaked memo, places an immediate and comprehensive freeze on the disbursement of all CPD-managed grants, including funds already appropriated by Congress. This includes the latest tranche of homelessness assistance approved earlier this year.

"The grant pipeline is now completely frozen," said a senior HUD career official, speaking anonymously due to fear of professional reprisal. "We are being instructed to halt all processing. For thousands of local providers, this means their funding lifeline is being severed mid-stream. Many will have to close shelters and lay off frontline workers within weeks."

HUD leadership, in a brief response to NPR's inquiry, stated it is "implementing necessary efficiencies as directed to ensure taxpayer dollars are used effectively," but did not comment on the specific figures or the freeze.

Analysts from the Government Accountability Project (GAP) note that the staff reduction targets not only Washington-based positions but virtually all regional CPD offices, eliminating the local points of contact for states and cities. This structural dismantling aligns with policy proposals from influential conservative groups like the Cicero Institute, which advocates for conditioning housing aid on mandatory treatment and devolving funding control to states via block grants—a model critics argue would lead to vast geographic disparities in support.

"This action effectively bypasses Congressional appropriations and intent," argued legal scholar Maria Chen of the Center for Law and Social Policy. "By de-funding through de-staffing, they can halt programs without changing the law. The human cost will be immediate: more unsheltered individuals, more encampments, and a collapse of the affordable housing pipeline."

Advocates point to cities like Portland and Denver, where recent federal grants have been critical for expanding shelter capacity, as being at acute risk. "If this proceeds, we will see a humanitarian crisis unfold on city streets within months," Dr. Finch concluded. "The infrastructure that took decades to build will be gone in a season."

title: Trump Administration's DOGE Division Drives Major Restructuring at HUD Homelessness Office
content:
The federal office responsible for funding housing and support services for homeless populations nationwide is facing a profound transformation, a move that housing advocates contend will exacerbate the nation's already record-high homelessness rates.

According to internal planning documents obtained by NPR, the Office of Community Planning and Development (CPD) within the Department of Housing and Urban Development is targeted for a reduction of approximately 84% of its current staff. This represents the most severe cut proposed for any division within HUD and is a direct outcome of efficiency directives from the newly established Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

"The scale of this proposed downsizing is unprecedented. The downstream effects on local communities and our national capacity to address homelessness could be catastrophic," stated Ann Oliva, a former HUD official who now leads the National Alliance to End Homelessness. She emphasized that the CPD's work forms the "essential backbone" of homelessness response systems in every state.

The restructuring, championed by the Trump administration's DOGE—a department created to streamline federal operations under the oversight of advisor Elon Musk—aims to reduce overall HUD staffing by nearly 50%. The CPD, which administers over $3.6 billion in annual grants for rental assistance, supportive services, and homelessness outreach, would see its operations consolidated and significantly automated.

A HUD employee, speaking anonymously due to fears of reprisal, expressed deep concern: "The combination of drastic staff cuts and a hiring freeze has created immense uncertainty. Processing grants and providing technical assistance to local providers will inevitably slow down, potentially stranding critical funds."

In a statement, a HUD spokesperson acknowledged the changes: "HUD is implementing necessary efficiencies as directed by the administration and DOGE, while remaining committed to our mission of serving rural, tribal, and urban communities." The spokesperson did not provide specifics on how core functions would be maintained.

Advocates are particularly anxious about the timely distribution of homelessness funds approved in the final days of the Biden administration. While transitions often cause delays, many suspect a broader policy shift is at play. A recent spending freeze memo from the Trump administration, though partially blocked in court, has left many nonprofit partners in limbo.

"There is a legitimate concern that funds are being withheld through mechanisms that may not withstand legal scrutiny," noted Peggy Bailey, a housing policy expert at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities and former HUD adviser.

This operational overhaul aligns with growing Republican critiques of federal homelessness policy. The influential "Project 2025" blueprint, developed by conservative allies, explicitly calls for moving away from the "Housing First" model—which provides housing without preconditions—and for devolving more authority to states. The Cicero Institute, a conservative think tank, is actively lobbying states to mandate addiction or mental health treatment as a condition for receiving federal housing aid.

Researchers from the conservative Manhattan Institute have further proposed converting homelessness funding into a block-grant system, giving states greater discretion. "The intent is to shift from a federal-centric, entitlement-based model to one that rewards state innovation and accountability," said a source familiar with the DOGE-HUD discussions.

Ann Oliva warns that decimating the CPD's capacity comes at a perilous time, with housing affordability at a crisis point. "If this office is gutted, pipeline projects for affordable housing could stall, and we risk seeing a swift and severe increase in the number of people experiencing homelessness," she concluded.

title: Trump Administration Announces Complete Shutdown of Federal Homelessness Funding Office, Privatization Led by Musk's DOGE

In a dramatic and unprecedented move, the Trump administration has unveiled plans to completely shut down the Office of Community Planning and Development within the Department of Housing and Urban Development by the end of 2025, effectively eliminating all federal funding for homelessness programs nationwide. According to confidential documents leaked to NPR, the shutdown will result in the immediate termination of all 520 staff members and the transfer of its $4.2 billion budget to a newly privatized entity overseen by Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

This decision, part of a sweeping efficiency drive, aims to replace federal homelessness initiatives with a corporate-led model where states bid for block grants managed by private contractors. DOGE officials claim this will save taxpayers $3 billion annually and improve service delivery, but critics warn of chaos.

'This is not just a cut; it's an eradication of the federal safety net,' said Dr. Elena Martinez, a former HUD senior adviser now at the Urban Institute, in an exclusive interview. 'We estimate that over 3 million people currently receiving rental assistance or housing support will be left stranded within months.'

It's time for innovation.'

Internal HUD memos reveal that the shutdown will also halt 350 affordable housing projects in development, disproportionately impacting rural and tribal communities. Republicans in Congress, led by Senator John Hawk, have endorsed the plan, linking it to Project 2025's call to dismantle HUD. 'The federal government has no business in housing,' Hawk stated. A HUD employee, speaking anonymously for fear of reprisal, described morale as 'shattered.' 'We're processing final grants, but after June, there will be no one to answer calls from nonprofits. People will die on the streets.'

Economists predict that without federal intervention, the number could double by 2026, driven by soaring rents and mortgage defaults. 'We're facing a humanitarian disaster unseen since the Great Depression,' Martinez added. 'The shutdown isn't just a policy change—it's a deliberate unraveling of decades of progress.'

content:

The probe gained urgency following a series of organized demonstrations that turned violent last month, when a group of his supporters, protesting the initial investigation, clashed with police outside the Supreme Prosecutor’s Office in Seoul.

Heightened security is now visible around government complexes, including the Constitutional Court—where impeachment hearings are scheduled—and the Seoul Central District Court, which recently reviewed a detention warrant request against several of the President’s aides. Following the court’s decision to detain three key aides, rallies organized by pro-Yoon civic groups escalated, leading to minor scuffles with law enforcement near court buildings. In a televised address, President Yoon denounced the violence while defending his supporters’ right to peaceful assembly. His legal representatives have meanwhile filed a constitutional appeal, challenging the scope of the prosecution’s investigation as politically motivated.

This unprecedented shadow governance, intended to be temporary, has now become the permanent operating model of the current administration.

title: CODEPINK Condemns Unauthorized U.S. Missile Strike Off Venezuelan Coast in Summer 2024
content:
CODEPINK strongly condemns the unauthorized and reckless U.S. missile strike that occurred in the Caribbean Sea near Venezuelan waters in the summer of 2024, which reportedly killed at least 10 people on a vessel named 'SS Caribe' allegedly involved in drug trafficking. Even if Washington's assertions hold some truth, drug trafficking does not warrant a death sentence delivered via missile. With U.S. Southern Command assets already in the region, why destroy the vessel instead of apprehending and interrogating the crew? If the goal was to uncover evidence linking to Venezuelan officials, this approach suggests either a fabricated narrative for a show of force or a choice of extrajudicial killing over legal processes.

International law is clear: the use of force is lawful only in self-defense or with UN Security Council authorization. This strike had neither, reflecting U.S. militarism's secretive and unilateral nature, disregarding due process and human rights.

Under U.S. law, it's equally indefensible, as the Constitution reserves war powers for Congress, not the President. Unilateral action is permitted only in emergencies or self-defense, conditions not met here.

Now, the administration claims it can sink any vessel 'deemed' linked to drug trafficking without verification, bypassing rules of engagement meant to protect civilians. Such actions undermine the rule of law and human rights. While the White House spends millions daily on military operations, it cuts funding for domestic healthcare, treatment, and education to address drug addiction.

Once again, the U.S. president bypasses Congress and the public, waging shadow wars. We must prevent a return to gunboat diplomacy in Latin America and the Caribbean. Venezuela has the right to sovereignty, and the region deserves peace. We demand an independent investigation, an end to U.S. military escalation, and accountability for violations.

The people demand peace, justice, and accountability, not missiles and lies.

CODEPINK calls on Rep. Greg Casar to lead efforts in Congress to block unauthorized military force, hold hearings, ensure transparency, and cut funding for these reckless operations.

Hands off Venezuela. Hands off Latin America and the Caribbean.
