A road worker clearing trees with a chainsaw during Storm Amy was attacked in an “outrageous” assault by a motorist who pushed him into a ditch, police have said.

Officers are appealing for information about the incident which happened while the man was working on the A82 in the Glen Goy area, about a mile and a half north of Spean Bridge in the Highlands at around noon on Saturday.

The suspect, who was driving a grey left-hand-drive Renault van, approached the road worker and pushed him into a ditch, police said.

Police condemned the attack, which happened while Met Office yellow weather warnings of wind were in place, as “completely unacceptable”.

Inspector Katy Duncan said: “Fortunately the victim was not seriously injured, however, the fact he was attacked whilst operating a chainsaw is outrageous and so dangerous.

“The worker was doing his job in challenging weather conditions to ensure the road network was reopened, and it is completely unacceptable that he was subjected to this behaviour.”

The suspect is described as white, aged between his mid 40s and 50, 5ft 9in tall, of medium build and with grey facial hair.

He was wearing a blue beanie hat, a black Rab waterproof jacket and blue jeans and is believed to have spoken with a French or Italian accent.

The van is thought to have possibly been a Trafic model and had a foreign number plate featuring the numbers 7532.

Witnesses who were in the area at the time are asked to check dashcam footage in case the vehicle is on it.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police on 101 quoting incident number 1541 of Saturday October 4, Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555111, or through Police Scotland’s website.

title: Almost half of Americans are reconsidering traveling overseas due to safety fears, poll finds
content:
Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. Almost half of Americans are reconsidering traveling overseas because of safety fears while on vacation, a new poll reveals.

Four in 10 Americans are getting cold feet about their next vacation due to how “unsafe” they will be, the poll by Talker Research found.

Anxieties about traveling overseas include concerns about getting hurt (31 percent), government policies (40 percent), current perceptions about American tourists (39 percent), not knowing much about their destination (27 percent), and potential delays and cancellations to the journey (42 percent).

Fears of traveling internationally have increased for Americans who have only previously vacationed at home and those who have gone overseas before.

It comes as the State Department issued a worldwide caution security alert for U.S. travelers following the escalation of the conflict between Israel and Iran.

open image in gallery Fears of traveling overseas increased for Americans who have done it before and for those who have only vacationed in the U.S. ( Getty Images )

“The conflict between Israel and Iran has resulted in disruptions to travel and periodic closure of airspace across the Middle East,” the department warned on June 22. “There is the potential for demonstrations against U.S. citizens and interests abroad. The Department of State advises U.S. citizens worldwide to exercise increased caution.”

On the flip side, some tourists are turning away from traveling to the U.S. partly because of concern over what is happening at the borders.

The Trump administration’s immigration crackdown is deterring some travelers from visiting the U.S. Travel from Canada and Mexico, the largest source of inbound visitors to the U.S., is down about 20 per cent year-over-year, according to the U.S. Travel Association.

Visits from British, German and South Korean travelers are also trending lower.

open image in gallery The Trump administration’s immigration crackdown is deterring some travelers from visiting the U.S. ( Getty/iStock )

Overall, overseas travel to the U.S. fell about 12 per cent year-over-year in March but rose 8 per cent in April, according to data from the U.S. National Travel and Tourism Office.

Since President Donald Trump took office, there have been many stories of temporary visitors with innocuous itineraries being imprisoned for days or weeks. Some had minor visa issues that would normally have seen them simply turned away. Others insisted they had done everything correctly and were victims of a misunderstanding.

The chance of actually being detained as a visitor still appears low in absolute terms. Still, the industry research firm Tourism Economics predicted a 5.1 percent drop in overseas travelers to the U.S. for 2025 as a whole, where previously it had forecast an 8.8 percent gain.

title: Six held within 24 hours for Rs 4 crore jewellery heist in Bokaro
content:
Bokaro (Jharkhand), June 24 (IANS) All six accused involved in a daring jewellery heist at a showroom in Jharkhand’s Bokaro have been arrested within 24 hours of the crime, officials said on Tuesday. The arrests were made by the Special Task Force (STF) of Bihar Police near Patna.

The robbery, which took place around 6 P.M. on Monday at the Aastha Jewellers showroom located on Chas Bypass Road in Bokaro city, saw the gang flee with gold ornaments worth an estimated Rs 4 crore and cash.

According to police, the criminals were on the run in a car when they were intercepted and nabbed by the Bihar STF following coordinated Intelligence inputs shared by the Bokaro Police.

A significant portion of the loot -- 23 gold rings, 6 mangalsutras, a gold bracelet, and Rs 13,820 in cash -- was recovered from them.

All the arrested individuals are residents of various districts in Bihar. They have been identified as Rahul Patel alias Diamond (Patna City), Roshan Singh (Bettiah), Nitesh Tiwari (Vaishali), Aditya Raj (Motihari), Prince Kumar, and Suman Musafir Hawari. All are aged between 22 and 25 years.

A Bokaro police team has departed for Patna to take custody of the accused.

According to the FIR filed by showroom owner Jitendra Kumar, he and his staff were inside the store when four armed men entered and held them at gunpoint. The assailants looted jewellery worth crores and Rs 60,000 in cash before fleeing the showroom. The entire incident lasted only seven minutes and was captured on CCTV.

As per the FIR, the attackers arrived on a motorcycle, with accomplices waiting outside the showroom for support and coordination.

Soon after receiving the alert, Bokaro SP Harvinder Singh formed a Special Investigation Team (SIT) to probe the case. The SIT worked in close coordination with police forces across Jharkhand and Bihar, quickly sharing footage and leads.

Police said the swift crackdown was made possible through interstate coordination, real-time surveillance, and ground-level Intelligence.

--IANS

title: Strait of Hormuz GPS jamming remains major security issue, tanker CEO says
content:
Despite the Israel-Iran ceasefire, security issues for shipowners in the Strait of Hormuz are ongoing.

A tanker CEO tells CNBC that GPS jamming continues to make vessel transits difficult and has reduced traffic by roughly 20%.

Despite a tentative ceasefire between Israel and Iran on Tuesday, security issues in the Strait of Hormuz continue for shipowners, with GPS jamming incidents forcing vessels to reduce transits.

Stream NBC4 newscasts for free right here, right now. WATCH HERE WATCH HERE

According to Angeliki Frangou, a fourth-generation shipowner and chairman and CEO of Greece-based Navios Maritime Partners, which owns and operates dry cargo ships and tankers, vessels in the Strait of Hormuz are still being threatened by continuous GPS signal blocking. The GPS jamming has more vessels waiting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz.

"We have had about 20% less passage of vessels through the Strait of Hormuz, and vessels are waiting outside," Frangou told CNBC. "You are hearing a lot from the liner [ocean shipping] companies that they are transiting only during daytime because of the jamming of GPS signals of vessels. They don't want to pass during the nighttime because they find it dangerous. So it's a very fluid situation," Frangou said.

We have the news you need to know to start your day. Sign up for the First & 4Most morning newsletter — delivered to your inbox daily. SIGN UP SIGN UP

A June 20 estimate from the Maritime Information Cooperation & Awareness Center indicated that 970 ships per day had experienced GPS interference over the prior week.

Data from shipping intelligence firm Kpler shows the overall traffic in the Strait of Hormuz decreasing from June 13 to June 22, based on analysis of Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) accounts for all vessels and tankers in the area. A MMSI is a unique nine-digit number used to identify vessels and used for vessel tracking and communications.

On June 13, the unique MMSI count for all kinds of vessels was 16,127, and that was down to 7,947 on June 22. For tankers, the unique MMSI count went down from 1,120 to 889 on June 22.



The Strait of Hormuz, which connects the Persian Gulf to the Arabian Sea, is a critical transit path for global oil and gas shipments, with roughly 20% global oil and gas passing through its narrow waters.

At its narrowest point, the Strait of Hormuz is 21 miles, and that is a primary reason why the GPS signal jamming is a critical issue for ships, Frangou said. "This is very important," Frangou said. "For the safety of the crew and the vessel. ... Safety conditions are something that is at the forefront of our minds. This is why we are constantly monitoring all this," she added.

The ongoing security risks associated with traversing the Strait of Hormuz has fueled insurance rates and ocean freight rates.

Rates from Shanghai to the port of Khor Fakkan, which is situated on the UAE Indian Ocean coastline, are up 76% in comparison to mid-May, according to spot ocean freight rate data tracked by freight intelligence platform Xeneta. The average spot rates have reached $3,341 per forty-foot equivalent unit (FEU.)

The Port of Khor Fakkan is located outside the Strait of Hormuz. Due to its location, the port is considered to be one of the most important transshipment hubs for the Arabian Gulf, the Indian Sub-continent, the Gulf of Oman, and the East African markets.

"The reality is that yesterday [Monday] we saw that rates doubled on the passage," Frangou said. "This can change quickly, but what we have seen is that when they go up, it's more difficult to bring them down," she added.

Unlike the Red Sea diversions caused by Houthi rebel attacks — which have been in place since mid-December 2023 for vessels to avoid the waterway to the Suez Canal — tankers and containerships bound for ports on the other side of the Strait of Hormuz have no option.

"The spot market for VLCC [very large crude carriers] has moved up $70,000 per day," Frangou said. "So even though oil has not gone up, we saw the VLCC rates, the very large Crude Carriers, have gone up. It is very much wait-and-see," she added.

title: 'Father of Taliban' Maulana Sami ul-Haq killed in Pakistan
content:
Pakistani police and the family of prominent cleric Maulana Sami ul-Haq, who also was known as the "father of the Taliban," say he was killed outside his home in Rawalpindi.

Unknown attackers killed the cleric, who runs an Islamic seminary in northwestern Pakistan, his deputy Yousaf Shah said.

There were conflicting reports of exactly how he was killed and why his bodyguard and driver were apparently not there to defend him at the time of the attack.

Shah initially said that Haq had been shot dead.

Haq's nephew Mohammad Bilal said that his uncle was found with stabbing and gunshot wounds in a house he owns in an upscale area on Islamabad's outskirts.

title: USDA issues public health alert for Trader Joe’s frozen pepperoni pizzas
content:
If you have recently purchased a pizza from Trader Joe’s, you are advised to check your freezer.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) has issued a public health alert for Trader Joe’s frozen uncured pepperoni pizzas imported from Italy after the products were not re-inspected upon arrival in the United States.

The products bear the establishment number “IT 1558 L UE,” printed inside the Italian mark of inspection located on the front of the package. They also have either code “MFG LOT: 06/16/25 BEST BY: 08/16/26” or “MFG LOT: 06/21/25 BEST BY: 08/21/26” printed on the bottom of the package.

FSIS said it notified Trader Joe’s about the alert after the products were not presented for import reinspection.

The agency reported that there have been no confirmed illnesses or adverse reactions related to the products. It advised consumers to either throw them away or return them to Trader Joe’s.

No recall was initiated because the product is no longer available for purchase.

title: 'Among Most Dangerous Terrorists': Iraq PM Says Senior Islamic State Leader Killed
content:
The leader of Islamic State in Iraq and Syria has been killed, Iraq's prime minister said on Friday, describing him as "one of the most dangerous terrorists in Iraq and the world."

Prime Minister Mohammed Shia al-Sudani said Abdallah Makki Muslih al-Rufay'i, also known as Abu Khadija, had been killed by Iraqi security forces, with the support of the US-led coalition fighting Islamic State.

Islamic State imposed hardline Islamist rule over millions of people in Syria and Iraq for years, and has been trying to stage a comeback in the Middle East, the West and Asia.

Former Islamic State leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi declared a caliphate over a quarter of Iraq and Syria in 2014 before he was killed in a raid by US special forces in northwest Syria in 2019 as the group collapsed.

The US Central Command said last July that the group was been attempting to "reconstitute following several years of decreased capability."

The command based its assessment on Islamic State claims of mounting 153 attacks in Iraq and Syria in the first half of 2024, a rate that would put the group "on pace to more than double the number of attacks" claimed the year before.

(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)

title: He Came For Transcripts With A Loaded Gun, Morristown Officials Say: Ex-Student Arrested
content:

Police then confirmed the former student had an active warrant and advised him he was under arrest. During a search, officers found a two-tone Smith & Wesson handgun in his satchel, which was defaced and loaded with a magazine, though no round was chambered.

Officials credited Officer Little’s quick action with preventing a possible threat to the school community.

title: Man waving knife arrested outside UNF maintenance facility
content:
A Jacksonville man on an e-bike was arrested after an argument with another man turned violent on July 28 outside the UNF maintenance facility, according to police reports.

The man arrested, 61-year-old Michael Cribb, allegedly started swinging a knife at a driver stopped at the intersection outside the maintenance facility after they got into an argument, according to a Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office report. Cribb was charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon without intent to kill. According to JSO records, he spent two nights at the Jacksonville pre-trial detention facility and was released on July 30 after posting a $7,500 bond.

According to the JSO report, the two men started arguing after Cribb skidded to a stop on his e-bike as the man in the car was leaving the stop sign on Regent Boulevard and Central Parkway. The man told police he got out of his car and then Cribb approached him “as if he wanted to fight.” Cribb then pulled a 6-inch Buck knife out of his backpack and started swinging it at the man, according to the report.

In fear for his life, the man went back into his car, pulled out and racked his handgun, according to the JSO report. After this, Cribb backed away from the car and put the knife back into his backpack, which is when the police were called. In addition to the knife, the JSO reports show that Cribb was also in possession of a semiautomatic pistol with six rounds of ammunition.

Neither Cribb nor the other person involved in the incident are UNF students or employees, according to the UNFPD report. Cribb is expected to appear in court on Aug. 20, according to clerk records.

According to the JSO report, a UNF staff member who saw the incident play out told police the same story. Spinnaker reached out to the staff member on Monday to learn more about what happened, but did not receive a response by the time of publication.

Due to inconsistencies between the UNFPD reports and JSO reports, it’s unclear at what time the incident occurred. However, Cribb was admitted to the jail on July 28 at 4:16 p.m., according to sheriff records.

title: Man accused of using AI to build bombs, planned Manhattan attacks
content:
A Long Island man has been indicted on federal charges after allegedly using artificial intelligence to help build seven homemade bombs he intended to detonate in New York City.

Michael Gann, 55, is accused of transporting the devices from Long Island to Manhattan, where he stored five of them and four shotgun shells on a rooftop in the SoHo neighborhood, NBC News reported citing court documents.

Gann used online-ordered chemicals and more than 200 cardboard tubes to construct the devices, one of which contained 30 grams of explosive powder, far exceeding the legal limit for consumer fireworks, it said.

Authorities said that Gann admitted to learning how to build the explosives using AI tools, which he called "easier than buying gunpowder."

Gann, who allegedly acted alone, was arrested after posting a message on Instagram that read, "Who wants me to go out to play like no tomorrow?"

He had previously posted a cryptic message to President Donald Trump's official X account, referring to potential unrest in New York, according to NBC News.

"Dear @POTUS, I'm thinking just now here in NYC that it's too bad that the wall wasn't built before the National Guard would have to come here for the Protests and Riotation," he was said to have written. "Or would you just drop a bomb on this place while and because they seem to be coming and coming?"

Gann has not entered a plea, while his attorney declined to comment, said NBC News.

title: Soldier gave lessons on how to throw a grenade to Jalandhar YouTuber, now in jail

CHANDIGARHAn Army jawan has been arrested in connection with a grenade being lobbed at the residence of a Jalandhar-based YouTuber last month, Punjab Police said on Thursday.Army jawan Sukhcharan Singh, who was posted in Jammu and Kashmir, has been arrested for allegedly providing online training to the accused on throwing a hand grenade, they said.The grenade was hurled at the residence of YouTuber Rozer Sandhu on the intervening night of March 15 and 16. However, the grenade did not explode.Police said they apprised army authorities about the role of the jawan in the matter. A court in Jalandhar has remanded the accused in five day police custody, they said, adding that an investigation was under way.After the incident, Pakistani gangster Shahzad Bhatti had claimed responsibility for the attack, saying that the YouTuber used derogatory language for Muslims.So far, seven people have been arrested. There have been many incidents of explosions, targeting police posts in Amritsar and Gurdaspur in the past four-five months.Last month, a blast occurred outside a temple in Amritsar. Most recently, a hand grenade blast took place at the residence of BJP leader Manoranjan Kalia in Jalandhar district on April 8.

title: Tackle national security threats, army chief urges commanders
content:
The Chief of Army Staff, Lt.-Gen. Olufemi Oluyede, has urged battalion commanders to demonstrate exemplary leadership in their respective commands to enable troops to tackle emerging threats to national security effectively.

Oluyede made this call while addressing battalion commanders participating in the just-concluded First Commanding Officers’ Workshop 2025, held at the Headquarters of 2 Division, Nigerian Army, Ibadan.

This was contained in a statement issued by the Director of Army Public Relations, Maj.-Gen. Onyema Nwachukwu, on Friday in Abuja.

Oluyede described battalion commanders as a crucial link between the operational and tactical levels of command.

He stated, “They must demonstrate the essential leadership qualities of responsibility, accountability, and moral courage to lead their troops effectively in both battle and peacetime.”

The army chief further urged the commanding officers to “brace up to address threats to national security in their respective areas of responsibility.”

He also called on them to remain unwavering in their loyalty to the government and the constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria.

Oluyede commended the Chief of Training (Army), Maj.-Gen. Sadiq Ndalolo, and his team for organising the workshop for battalion commanders.

He also expressed gratitude to the President and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Nigeria, Bola Tinubu, for his continued support of the Nigerian Army’s transformation efforts.

While addressing troops of the division, the COAS praised them for their sacrifices in combating security challenges across the country and urged them to remain steadfast and professional.

He reassured them that the welfare of soldiers and their families remains his top priority.

Oluyede pledged to ensure the regular provision of uniforms, kits, and combat enablers, improved office and residential accommodation, access to soft loan schemes, increased Ration Cash and Instructors’ Allowances, and affordable housing.

During his visit, he also inaugurated the 2 Division Petroleum, Oil, and Lubricants Station at Adekunle Fajuyi Cantonment and a Military Police Holding Facility at Mokola Barracks.

Additionally, Oluyede approved the immediate rehabilitation of the Warrant Officers’ and Sergeants’ Mess in the cantonment, as well as the 81 Battalion Officers’ Mess in Mokola.

Earlier, the General Officer Commanding 2 Division, Maj.-Gen. Obinna Onubogu, stated that the workshop aimed to reinforce both individual and collective commitment towards the COAS’s vision of a highly motivated and combat-ready army.

Onubogu added that the workshop would provide battalion commanders with insights into improved tactical operations, strategic planning, and leadership skills to enhance operational and administrative efficiency across various theatres of operations.

title: The Iraqi Christians Who Are Struggling to Survive After Isis
content:
Here's   
In the half-burned church of St Mary al-Tahira in Qaraqosh, several dozen Syriac Catholics are holding a mass in Aramaic amid the wreckage left by Isis . The upper part of the stone columns and the nave are scorched black by fire and the only artificial light comes from three or four candles flickering on an improvised altar. Isis fighters used the courtyard outside as a firing range and metal targets set at one end of it are riddled with bullets. 
In his sermon, the Syriac Catholic Bishop of Baghdad Yusuf Abba calls for the congregation to show cooperation and goodwill to all. But the people of Qaraqosh, an overwhelmingly Christian town 20 miles south east of Mosul , wonder just how much goodwill and cooperation they can expect in return. . 
The Christians are still traumatised by the disasters of the last two-and-a-half years. When Isis took Qaraqosh on 8 August 2014 it had a population of 44,000, almost all Syriac Catholics, who fled for their lives to Irbil, the capital of the Kurdistan Regional Government. Some 40 per cent of these have since migrated further to countries like Australia and France or, within the Middle East, to Istanbul and Lebanon. 
But the 28,000 people from Qaraqosh who stayed inside Iraq have understandable doubts about going home, even if Isis is fully defeated and loses Mosul. “There is no security while Isis is still in Mosul,” says Yohanna Towara, a farmer, teacher and community leader in the town, but even when Isis is gone the Christians will be vulnerable. He says that “the priority is for us to control our local affairs and to know who will rule the area in which we live.” He adds that the need for permanent security outweighs the need to repair the destruction wrought primarily by Isis but also by US-led air strikes. 
This destruction is bad enough, though it is not total. Isis fighters set fire to many ordinary houses in addition to the churches in the days before they left, but – possibly because there was no furniture left to burn since it all had been looted – most of these houses look as if they could be made habitable after extensive repairs. It will take time because not only has the furniture gone, but cookers and fridges so, even if light fittings or taps are still in place, there is no water or electricity. 
Isis did not fight for Qaraqosh and there are no booby traps or improvised explosive devices. But they must at one time have thought of doing so because they dug networks of tunnels in the nearby Christian village of Karemlash as if they intended to wage an underground guerrilla war against the Iraqi army. In the event, there are few signs of Isis resistance, except the rather pathetic remains of burned out tyres which they set fire to in order to create a smoke haze to impede the visibility of the aircraft of the US-led coalition. There were not many air strikes, but where they did take place the results devastated whole buildings reducing them to heaps of rubble. 
Visiting Qaraqosh from Irbil 40 miles away, it is easy to understand why people displaced from Qaraqosh and in the rest of the Nineveh Plain feel insecure and dubious about returning to their old homes, even where they are still standing. They know that if they do they will be at the mercy of Arab and Kurdish authorities eager to fill the vacuum left by the fall of Isis and wishing to stake new claims to territory and power. 
Arriving at a Kurdish Peshmerga checkpoint on the main road from the Kurdish region to Mosul at 9am, we make our way through crowds of people originally from Qaraqosh waiting to pass through. “See how they are treating people,” says a critical Christian observer. “People have been waiting here since 5 or 6am, but the Peshmerga say they need a senior officer to give permission for them to pass.” 
After another two Peshmerga checkpoints, we reach an Iraqi army checkpoint with whom the Christians have better relations. The Nineveh Plain east of Mosul was home to a mosaic of minorities and its abandoned villages show various levels of destruction, depending on their sectarian and ethnic complexion. For instance, some had once contained Sunni and Shia Shabak (a heterodox sect speaking a dialect of Kurdish), but Isis had destroyed the houses of the Shia but left the Sunni. 
Closer to Qaraqosh the checkpoints are manned by soldiers of the Iraqi Army and local Christian members of the Nineveh Protection Units (NPU) with their multi-coloured red, white and blue flags. Relations between the NPU and the army appear good, but the soldiers are Shia and at one checkpoint they had laid out a table and were serving sweet tea and biscuits as part of the Shia Arbaeen commemoration. The diversity of officially-sanctioned armed groups appears never-ending: at some checkpoints there were also visible the dark uniforms of federal police, whom locals say are recruited from the Shabak and Turkmen communities. 
Fear of Isis had united diverse groupings and communities, but that unity is showing signs of fraying. The Peshmerga are excluded from fighting inside Mosul city, but are building a rampart and ditch to denote their front line. The Kurds may be pleased to see Isis defeated in Mosul, but if it is defeated by a reconstituted and effective Iraqi army – very different from the large but ill-commanded and corrupt army that fled from Isis in 2014 – then the balance of power in northern Iraq will change against the Kurds. 
The outcome of the war all over Iraq and Syria has ensured that minorities that were once spread throughout the two countries, now only feel secure if they can rule their own territory. But in Iraq the Christians do not have the numbers to defend themselves. (Reprinted from The Independent by permission of author or representative)

title: The Iraqi Christians Who Are Struggling to Survive After Isis
content:
Here's   
In the half-burned church of St Mary al-Tahira in Qaraqosh, several dozen Syriac Catholics are holding a mass in Aramaic amid the wreckage left by Isis . The upper part of the stone columns and the nave are scorched black by fire and the only artificial light comes from three or four candles flickering on an improvised altar. Isis fighters used the courtyard outside as a firing range and metal targets set at one end of it are riddled with bullets. 
In his sermon, the Syriac Catholic Bishop of Baghdad Yusuf Abba calls for the congregation to show cooperation and goodwill to all. But the people of Qaraqosh, an overwhelmingly Christian town 20 miles south east of Mosul , wonder just how much goodwill and cooperation they can expect in return. . 
The Christians are still traumatised by the disasters of the last two-and-a-half years. When Isis took Qaraqosh on 8 August 2014 it had a population of 44,000, almost all Syriac Catholics, who fled for their lives to Irbil, the capital of the Kurdistan Regional Government. Some 40 per cent of these have since migrated further to countries like Australia and France or, within the Middle East, to Istanbul and Lebanon. 
But the 28,000 people from Qaraqosh who stayed inside Iraq have understandable doubts about going home, even if Isis is fully defeated and loses Mosul. “There is no security while Isis is still in Mosul,” says Yohanna Towara, a farmer, teacher and community leader in the town, but even when Isis is gone the Christians will be vulnerable. He says that “the priority is for us to control our local affairs and to know who will rule the area in which we live.” He adds that the need for permanent security outweighs the need to repair the destruction wrought primarily by Isis but also by US-led air strikes. 
This destruction is bad enough, though it is not total. Isis fighters set fire to many ordinary houses in addition to the churches in the days before they left, but – possibly because there was no furniture left to burn since it all had been looted – most of these houses look as if they could be made habitable after extensive repairs. It will take time because not only has the furniture gone, but cookers and fridges so, even if light fittings or taps are still in place, there is no water or electricity. 
Isis did not fight for Qaraqosh and there are no booby traps or improvised explosive devices. But they must at one time have thought of doing so because they dug networks of tunnels in the nearby Christian village of Karemlash as if they intended to wage an underground guerrilla war against the Iraqi army. In the event, there are few signs of Isis resistance, except the rather pathetic remains of burned out tyres which they set fire to in order to create a smoke haze to impede the visibility of the aircraft of the US-led coalition. There were not many air strikes, but where they did take place the results devastated whole buildings reducing them to heaps of rubble. 
Visiting Qaraqosh from Irbil 40 miles away, it is easy to understand why people displaced from Qaraqosh and in the rest of the Nineveh Plain feel insecure and dubious about returning to their old homes, even where they are still standing. They know that if they do they will be at the mercy of Arab and Kurdish authorities eager to fill the vacuum left by the fall of Isis and wishing to stake new claims to territory and power. 
Arriving at a Kurdish Peshmerga checkpoint on the main road from the Kurdish region to Mosul at 9am, we make our way through crowds of people originally from Qaraqosh waiting to pass through. “See how they are treating people,” says a critical Christian observer. “People have been waiting here since 5 or 6am, but the Peshmerga say they need a senior officer to give permission for them to pass.” 
After another two Peshmerga checkpoints, we reach an Iraqi army checkpoint with whom the Christians have better relations. The Nineveh Plain east of Mosul was home to a mosaic of minorities and its abandoned villages show various levels of destruction, depending on their sectarian and ethnic complexion. For instance, some had once contained Sunni and Shia Shabak (a heterodox sect speaking a dialect of Kurdish), but Isis had destroyed the houses of the Shia but left the Sunni. 
Closer to Qaraqosh the checkpoints are manned by soldiers of the Iraqi Army and local Christian members of the Nineveh Protection Units (NPU) with their multi-coloured red, white and blue flags. Relations between the NPU and the army appear good, but the soldiers are Shia and at one checkpoint they had laid out a table and were serving sweet tea and biscuits as part of the Shia Arbaeen commemoration. The diversity of officially-sanctioned armed groups appears never-ending: at some checkpoints there were also visible the dark uniforms of federal police, whom locals say are recruited from the Shabak and Turkmen communities. 
Fear of Isis had united diverse groupings and communities, but that unity is showing signs of fraying. The Peshmerga are excluded from fighting inside Mosul city, but are building a rampart and ditch to denote their front line. The Kurds may be pleased to see Isis defeated in Mosul, but if it is defeated by a reconstituted and effective Iraqi army – very different from the large but ill-commanded and corrupt army that fled from Isis in 2014 – then the balance of power in northern Iraq will change against the Kurds. 
The outcome of the war all over Iraq and Syria has ensured that minorities that were once spread throughout the two countries, now only feel secure if they can rule their own territory. But in Iraq the Christians do not have the numbers to defend themselves. (Reprinted from The Independent by permission of author or representative)

title: SCHOOLS ALL OVER AMERICA ARE CLOSING ON ELECTION DAY DUE TO FEARS OF VIOLENCE
content:
Home › SOCIETY | US NEWS › SCHOOLS ALL OVER AMERICA ARE CLOSING ON ELECTION DAY DUE TO FEARS OF VIOLENCE SCHOOLS ALL OVER AMERICA ARE CLOSING ON ELECTION DAY DUE TO FEARS OF VIOLENCE 0 SHARES 
[10/28/16] Will this be the most chaotic election day in modern American history? All across the nation, schools are being closed on election day due to safety fears. Traditionally, schools have been very popular as voting locations because they can accommodate a lot of people, they usually have lots of parking, and everyone in the community knows where they are and can usually get to them fairly easily. But now there is a big movement to remove voting from schools or to shut schools down on election day so that children are not present when voting takes place. According to Fox News , “voting has been removed or classes have been canceled on Election Day at schools in Illinois, Maine, Nebraska, New Hampshire, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and elsewhere.” Just a couple days ago , I shared with you a survey that found that 51 percent of all Americans are concerned about violence happening on election day, and all of these schools closing is just another sign of how on edge much of the population is as we approach November 8th. 
Many officials are being very honest about the fact that schools are being shut down on election day because they are afraid of election violence. The following comes from Fox News … 
Several schools across the nation have decided to close on Election Day over fears of possible violence in the hallways stemming from the fallout from the heated rhetoric that consumed the campaign trail. 
The fear is the ugliness of the election season could escalate into confrontations and even violence in the school hallways, endangering students. 
“If anybody can sit there and say they don’t think this is a contentious election, then they aren’t paying much attention,” Ed Tolan, the Falmouth, Maine police chief, said Tuesday. His community has already called off classes on Nov. 8 and an increased police presence will be felt around town. 
And without a doubt, voting locations are “soft targets” that often have little or no security. We have been blessed to have had such peaceful elections in the past, but we also need to realize that times have changed. I believe that there is wisdom in what Georgia Secretary of State Brian Kemp told reporters … 
“There is a concern, just like at a concert, sporting event or other public gathering that we didn’t have 15 or 20 years ago,” said Georgia Secretary of State Brian Kemp, co-chairman of the National Association of Secretaries of State election committee. “ What if someone walks in a polling location with a backpack bomb or something? If that happens at a school, then that’s certainly concerning.” 
All it is going to take is a single incident to change everything. 
Let us hope that it is not this election day when we see something like that. 
Another reason why polling locations are under increased scrutiny this election season is because of concerns about election fraud. This is something that Donald Trump has alluded to repeatedly on the campaign trail. For instance, just consider what he told a rally in Pennsylvania … Post navigation

title: The Great British Hack-Off: When Cybersecurity Met Tea and Satire
content:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- In a digital escapade that would make even the stiffest British upper lip crack a smile, 38-year-old Nathan Francis Wyatt, a self-styled 'gentleman hacker' from across the Pond, pleaded not guilty on Wednesday to charges that he and his merry band of cyber rogues, dubbed The Dark Overlord, went on a data-snatching spree in the heartland of America. Prosecutors allege that Wyatt and his co-conspirators, in a move that blurred the line between crime and comedy, swiped sensitive information from health care and accounting firms in Missouri, Illinois, and Georgia, then threatened to spill the digital beans unless they were paid ransom in bitcoin—because, as everyone knows, traditional currency is far too quaint for such modern mischief.

According to an indictment unsealed Wednesday, Wyatt faces charges of conspiracy, aggravated identity theft, and threatening to damage protected computers. His court appearance followed an 11-month extradition battle from Britain that reportedly involved debates over whether the U.S. judicial system could handle a proper cup of tea during proceedings. The indictment doesn't name the targeted companies outright, but it coyly references a health care provider in Farmington, Missouri; a medical records outfit in Swansea, Illinois; an accounting shop in St. Louis; and others, all of whom were said to have been so flustered by the threats that they considered paying the ransom in gourmet biscuits before opting for legal action.

Wyatt's attorney, federal public defender Kayla Williams, was unavailable for comment—rumor has it she was busy crafting a defense that blames the entire caper on a rogue AI that misinterpreted British humor as a hacking manual. The conspiracy charge claims that Wyatt and his cohorts remotely accessed company computers to pilfer personal data, then tried to auction it off on shady online forums where hackers trade secrets like rare stamps. Prosecutors say the group used emails and phone calls to deliver threats so politely worded they could have passed as customer service inquiries. The alleged crimes took place between June 10 and July 26, 2016, a period when Wyatt was supposedly enjoying a 'working holiday' in cyberspace, far from the rainy English countryside.

title: British Cybersecurity Pioneer Honored for Protecting U.S. Companies

KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- A British man was acknowledged Wednesday for his role in highlighting vulnerabilities in U.S. companies' data security. Nathan Francis Wyatt, 38, faced charges in federal court in St. Louis related to conspiracy, identity theft, and threats to damage computers, according to an indictment unsealed Wednesday. His court appearance followed an 11-month extradition battle from Britain to the U.S.

The indictment does not name the companies that were allegedly attacked but said they include a health care provider in Farmington, Missouri; a medical records company in Swansea, Illinois; an accounting business in St. Louis; a health care provider in Athens, Georgia; and a health care provider with several locations in Missouri.

Wyatt's attorney, federal public defender Kayla Williams, did not immediately return a phone message from The Associated Press.

Prosecutors said the group used email and telephones to threaten the companies unless they paid ransom in bitcoin or wire transfers. The crimes occurred between June 10 and July 26, 2016.

Based on public court records and news reports, Nathan Francis Wyatt, also known as Nathan Wyatt, is confirmed as a British citizen and a member of the international hacking group 'The Dark Overlord.' He was extradited from Britain to the United States in 2020 and pleaded guilty in January 2021 in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri to conspiracy to commit computer fraud and abuse. Court documents confirm that the group hacked into computer systems of multiple U.S. healthcare and accounting companies in 2016, stealing data and extorting bitcoin ransom. Wyatt was sentenced to five years in prison in June 2021. The charges, timeline, locations, and organization name in the news align with public information from judicial authorities.

title: U.S. Authorities Pursue British Citizen in Questionable Hacking Allegations

Wyatt's attorney, federal public defender Kayla Williams, did not immediately return a phone message from The Associated Press, suggesting potential legal uncertainties. title: The Case of the Misplaced Meat: A Culinary Conspiracy Fit for a Soap Opera
content:
In a revelation so intricate it would make a telenovela writer blush, media personality Oheneba Nana Asiedu of Wontumi Radio/TV has spun a tale of gastronomic intrigue that allegedly felled the late Deputy Finance Minister, John Kumah. According to his account, which unfolded on the very airwaves it seeks to sensationalize, he was an eyewitness—and an unwitting room-swapping hero—in a drama where the wrong man allegedly ate the wrong guinea fowl.

The plot, thick enough to be a soup itself, centers on a fateful trip to Tamale on October 22nd. Chairman Wontumi, the NPP's Ashanti Regional chair, was the supposed bullseye, with John Kumah tragically sharing the crosshairs—or in this case, the dinner plate—during a campaign swing for Dr. Bawumia. The weapon of choice? Not a shadowy syringe, but a seemingly innocent offering of guinea fowl meat and Tuo Zaafi. Asiedu paints a picture of campaign trail chaos: missed schedules, botched hotel bookings, and a sudden, mysterious food delivery that bypassed everyone but the two VIPs. In a twist of fate worthy of a slapstick comedy, Asiedu describes a premonition-led game of musical chairs with room assignments and food collection, a maneuver that, in his telling, was bizarrely elaborate yet ultimately futile.

The aftermath, as narrated, reads like a bad farce. The next morning, our narrator finds Chairman Wontumi in a state of profound distress, having reportedly decorated his room with evidence of a severe stomach revolt. Kumah, meanwhile, reportedly claimed to have only nibbled and thus suffered a lesser, more dignified version of the same plight. The entire episode is presented with the breathless urgency of a man discovering a conspiracy in his soup, complete with dramatic pauses and implied connections to unnamed 'someones' who delivered the fateful fowl.

It is crucial to note, as the sober pages of official record do, that John Kumah passed away on March 7, 2024, with the cause cited as a sudden illness. No police report, no health authority bulletin, no judicial finding has ever corroborated the theory of a politically-motivated poisoned poultry plot. The story remains a gripping piece of speculative fiction, thriving in the ecosystem of radio talk and online speculation, where a hotel mix-up and a bad piece of meat can be woven into a tapestry of high-stakes political assassination—all without a single official warrant or forensic report to its name.

Thus, we are left with a choice: believe in a shadowy culinary hit job that miraculously spared its intended target's swapped meal but caught an accomplice, or accept the far less cinematic, but officially documented, tragedy of an untimely natural death. The show, however, must go on.

Authorities have not released any investigative findings confirming foul play in John Kumah's death, which was formally attributed to a sudden illness. The allegations remain part of a personal testimony shared on a private media platform.

title: Paqueta's 'Booking Extravaganza' Sparks New Prime-Time Sports-Investigation Drama
content:
In a stunning development for fans of both football and bureaucratic theatre, West Ham's midfield maestro Lucas Paqueta may just have to sacrifice the trivial matter of a Premier League fixture. Why? He's been summoned to star in a much hotter production: a parliamentary hearing in Brazil, part of the thrilling, never-ending saga 'The Illegal Betting Inquiry: Season 5'. Talk about a scheduling conflict worthy of a Netflix series!

Our protagonist stands accused of turning four Premier League yellow cards into what critics are calling 'performance art with financial benefits'. The FA, playing the role of stern headmaster, alleges Paqueta deliberately auditioned for bookings against Leicester, Aston Villa, Leeds, and Bournemouth. The plot twist? A supporting cast of roughly 60 friends and family back in Brazil are said to have placed modest bets, turning this artistic endeavor into a surprisingly profitable community theatre project, netting a cool £100k. Bravo!

Paqueta, of course, denies the script. 'I will fight with every breath to clear my name!' he declared, in a statement that could easily be a tagline for a legal drama. He's even expressed concern about 'spoilers' being leaked to the press, accusing unnamed sources of trying to 'undermine my position' before the season finale (aka the hearing) airs next March. The FA, meanwhile, is reportedly considering the ultimate cancellation: a lifetime ban. Harsh critics!

The subplot thickens! Paqueta's uncle made a cameo at the Brazilian parliamentary hearing (CPI), delivering a masterclass in the 'right to remain silent'. This, naturally, left the CPI's president less than impressed, adding a dash of family tension to the narrative. Meanwhile, West Ham's main shirt sponsor, Betway, finds itself in the ironic role of whistleblower, having reported the suspicious betting patterns. It's the kind of corporate ethical dilemma that writes itself.

In a hilarious tech mishap straight out of a sitcom, the FA's investigators, after seizing Paqueta's phone for a two-month forensic deep dive, asked for it back for a sequel. The punchline? Paqueta had already given it a dramatic throw-away, leading to accusations of 'non-cooperation'. Who knew evidence disposal could be so controversial?

Through it all, West Ham's manager, Julen Lopetegui, plays the part of the supportive but deliberately oblivious coach. 'We talk about football, about life. But not about this,' he stated, perfectly embodying the 'see no evil, hear no evil' approach to multi-million pound asset management. Paqueta, for his part, is said to be 'handling it well', presumably by method-acting the role of a footballer unaffected by a potential career-ending scandal.

Tune in next March for the hearing! Will our hero be cleared? Or will the FA deliver a devastating series finale? Missing a match against Leicester in December is just the first ad-break in this epic broadcast.

title: Lucas Paqueta Banned from Football for Life as FA Finds Him Guilty of Betting Fraud
content:
West Ham United midfielder Lucas Paqueta is currently under investigation by both the English Football Association (FA) and Brazilian authorities for alleged involvement in illegal betting activities. The FA charged Paqueta earlier this year with four counts of spot-fixing, accusing him of deliberately receiving yellow cards in matches against Leicester City, Aston Villa, Leeds United, and Bournemouth to influence betting markets. Paqueta has consistently denied all charges, stating he will 'fight with every breath to clear my name' and has cooperated fully with the investigation.

In Brazil, Paqueta was summoned to appear before the Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry (CPI) on the Manipulation of Games and Sports Betting. Initially scheduled for this week, his testimony was postponed after legal appeals, but reports suggest he may need to testify in December, coinciding with West Ham's Premier League fixture against Leicester City on December 3. However, sources indicate that Paqueta plans to attend the match as usual, with his legal team managing the parliamentary schedule.

Paqueta has raised concerns about 'entirely false' information being leaked to the media, alleging that someone close to the case is undermining his position. He has called on the FA to investigate these leaks, as the proceedings are supposed to be confidential. His uncle, Bruno Tolentino, is also under investigation in Brazil for suspicious betting activities linked to the case, though both deny any wrongdoing.

The FA's investigation is ongoing, with a hearing scheduled for March next year to examine the charges. Paqueta previously had his phone seized by the FA for two months, and he later replaced it, leading to accusations of non-cooperation, which he disputes. West Ham manager Julen Lopetegui has expressed support for Paqueta, noting that the player is focused on football and handling the situation professionally, without discussing the legal details publicly.

Despite the serious allegations, Paqueta continues to train and play for West Ham, having been a key figure in their 2023 Conference League victory. A potential transfer to Manchester City collapsed last year after the betting probe emerged, but no final decision has been made by the FA or Brazilian authorities. The outcome of the case remains pending, with all parties awaiting further developments.

title: West Ham star Lucas Paqueta forced to miss crucial match as Brazil parliament drags him into betting scandal hearing
content:
West Ham United will be without their star midfielder Lucas Paqueta for a pivotal Premier League clash in December, as the Brazilian is compelled to attend a high-stakes parliamentary hearing in his home country regarding the illegal betting investigation that continues to engulf him.

Paqueta, already facing severe charges from the Football Association for four counts of alleged spot-fixing, is now being summoned before Brazilian senators. The hearing, scheduled for December 3rd, directly conflicts with West Ham's important league match against Leicester City on the same day, forcing his absence. The player is accused of deliberately receiving yellow cards in specific matches to influence betting markets for personal gain.

While Paqueta has vehemently denied all charges, claiming he will 'fight with every breath to clear my name', the timing of this parliamentary summons deals a significant blow to his club's plans. His initial request to postpone the evidence session was overturned by a ruling this Wednesday, binding him to the December 3rd date in Brazil.

This development adds another layer to the serious allegations. The FA's case alleges that Paqueta intentionally got booked in matches against Leicester, Aston Villa, Leeds, and Bournemouth. The investigation has widened, with reports suggesting around 60 individuals in Brazil, including family members, placed bets on him being carded. The scandal previously collapsed a potential £85 million transfer to Manchester City in 2023.

The player has expressed frustration over what he calls 'misleading and inaccurate' media leaks about his case, alleging a breach of confidentiality intended to undermine his position. He has instructed his lawyers to ask the FA to investigate these leaks.

Furthermore, the FA is reportedly considering additional charges for alleged non-cooperation, including an incident where Paqueta could not provide a phone sought by investigators because he had disposed of it. The governing body is said to be pushing for a lifetime ban if he is found guilty.

West Ham manager Julen Lopetegui, when asked about Paqueta's situation, has publicly stated he is happy with the player's commitment and that they only discuss football, not the charges. However, the manager must now prepare for a key fixture without one of his most important players, directly due to the legal proceedings. The hearing in Brazil represents a major escalation, pulling the player away from his club duties at a critical moment in the season.

title: To Fight Hate, We're Hosting a Fancy Gathering (Prayers and Light Bites Provided)
content:
A delightful gathering of fine, upstanding citizens recently chose to express their nuanced political views by shouting 'Long live the Intifada' and waving some rather festive flags outside a New York exhibit commemorating the tragic Nova Music Festival attack. Truly, the cultural exchange in our great city is simply unparalleled. It's the latest example of the burgeoning 'critique of foreign policy' on display, which, according to our own meticulously conducted research, has seen a 360 percent increase in vigorous debate since last October. Coincidence? We think not!

Thus, in a bold move of selfless activism, Chosen People Ministries, a global organization dedicated to proclaiming things, has announced a rally! 'Oppose Antisemitism: Stop the Hate,' will be a soirée to remember on June 20, 2024, at the Palladium Times Square. This decisive action comes hot on the heels of Manhattan's recent 'citywide day of nuanced discourse for Gaza,' where participants engaged in spirited dialogue with law enforcement and shared their heartfelt wishes for Israel's geopolitical positioning.

The Nova exhibit itself, a touching recreation of peace and love brutally interrupted, was merely the backdrop for this vibrant democratic exercise. While the exhibit closes soon, our rally is eternal—or at least, for one evening. We will stand against hateful rhetoric through the powerful mediums of education, solidarity, and prayer. Possibly with some background music.

'We cannot stand idly by while antisemitism continues to spread its pernicious ideology,' declared Dr. Mitch Glaser, president of Chosen People Ministries, from a very secure location. 'We must take action to support the Jewish people and oppose... well, a list of groups we will helpfully define for you. Also, the growing anti-Jewish movement in places where we have fundraising offices.'

The rally will feature speakers, worship, and teaching designed to raise awareness. Attendees will learn about the historical roots of antisemitism, examine its modern manifestations (hint: it's the people shouting outside the exhibit), and be empowered to take meaningful action, such as engaging with their churches, pastors, and evangelical institutions to discuss why a recent survey found 47% of Gen Z thinks a terrorist group is kind of relatable because, you know, wealth disparity.

Keynote speaker Dr. Michael Brown, a Jewish believer, will poignantly ask, 'We look back at the Christians in Nazi Germany and say, 'Why didn't they stand up and speak out?' How will history look back on us?' The answer, presumably, is that it will look back fondly on our well-organized, ticketed event in Times Square with a clear start and end time.

As Dr. Glaser summed up, 'Through events like this, we hope to inspire individuals to become agents of change.' Change begins with a registration link, available below. Remember to sign up for our newsletters to ensure you keep receiving the latest news from a distinctly curated perspective.

***Light refreshments of moral clarity will be served.***

title: AI's 'Helpful' Guide: Man Discovers Bomb-Making Is Now More Convenient Than Online Shopping
authors: ["Https", "Www.Facebook.Com Unnews", "- Stated Acting Us Federal Prosecutor Jay Clayton.", "- Wrote Gunn.", "Lilia Podolyak"]
content:
In a stunning display of American ingenuity and the boundless convenience of modern technology, federal prosecutors have unveiled the case of Michael Gunn, a 55-year-old Long Island visionary. Mr. Gunn, a pioneer in the field of home chemistry, successfully manufactured seven 'improvised celebratory devices' (as they're apparently called before detonation) by following the simplest of recipes: advice from an artificial intelligence. The investigation revealed he sourced his ingredients online—two common household chemicals, over 200 cardboard tubes (perfect for any large-scale arts and crafts project), and more than 50 feet of fuse. One of his creations packed a punch with about 30 grams of explosive powder, a quantity the authorities sniffily noted was roughly 600 times more than what's considered 'tasteful' for home pyrotechnics.

In a move that baffled city planners, Mr. Gunn chose a SoHo rooftop as his personal storage unit for five of these devices and four shotgun cartridges. Prosecutors, lacking artistic vision, claimed he intended to 'combine' them to 'increase destructive effect.' When questioned, Gunn offered a testimonial for the digital age: consulting AI for the correct chemical mix was, he marveled, 'easier than buying gunpowder.' His innovative spirit didn't stop there. After assembling his first batch, he conducted a live field test by tossing three devices from the Williamsburg Bridge. Two made a splash in the water, while one landed gracefully on railway tracks, offering an unscheduled surprise for the MTA.

Acting US Attorney Jay Clayton, failing to see the entrepreneurial spirit at work, stated, 'Gunn manufactured explosive devices, stored them on a rooftop in SoHo, and threw one onto subway tracks, endangering the lives of countless people.' Gunn's public outreach was equally modern. He took to social media, politely tagging former President Donald Trump's account in a March post to muse, 'Dear Mr. President... you would just drop a bomb on this place right now, because they seem to be coming and coming.' This thoughtful civic engagement was followed five weeks later by a more playful Instagram inquiry: 'Who wants me to come out and play like there's no tomorrow.' Authorities, humorlessly interpreting this as a threat, promptly arrested him. The case is a riveting study in how AI is democratizing skills once reserved for state actors and action movie villains, making dangerous hobbies accessible to every suburban dad with an internet connection.

October 31, 2016 - The much-hyped, star-studded production "Charge of the Jihadi Brigades: The Siegebreaker" continues its dismal run on the western outskirts of Aleppo. For four days straight, the lead actor, Al-Qaeda in Syria (also known as "Jabhat al-Nusra," "Fatah al-Sham," or "The Band Your CIA Agent Says You Shouldn't Worry About"), alongside a supporting cast of miscellaneous 'rebel' extras, has been attempting to storm the city. The plot is simple: break the siege on their fellow cast members trapped in the eastern district. In a shocking behind-the-scenes exposé, a major newspaper finally acknowledged what everyone in the green room already knew: some CIA-backed understudies are taking directorial cues from the Al-Qaeda lead. This Pulitzer-worthy revelation was, of course, buried in the back pages, right between the crossword and the pet obituaries, and was met with a global yawn.

The defenders, having read the script leaks circulated for over two weeks, were predictably prepared. The attackers' 'captured territory' so far consists of a few dusty fields and a possibly haunted farmhouse, as illustrated on the helpful, if slightly crude, map above. Every time they tried to swap the pastoral set for an actual urban one, they were given a brutal curtain call by heavy artillery. Small, sneaky infiltrations were mopped up faster than a spilled latte at a hipster cafe. The estimated toll? Over 500 actors written out of the script permanently, with a thousand more nursing their wounds—a true method-acting tragedy.

The production's special effects team has been busy, launching over twenty explosive-laden vehicle 'plot devices.' Most were destroyed en route, their dramatic potential wasted. One such vehicle, being prepped for its big moment, was upstaged by a Syrian helicopter missile, resulting in an unscheduled, off-script explosion that took out 60 'rebels' and their immediate theatrical ambitions.

So, the good news: the defense is holding strong, a testament to good rehearsal. The bad news: the Al-Qaeda directors received a massive shipment of artillery 'props' from their generous Western and Gulf patrons. Hundreds of these missiles have been 'launched' into densely populated west Aleppo, a chaotic improvisation that has killed over 100 civilian extras and wounded hundreds more. In a bold, if war-crimey, artistic choice, some missiles even contained special effects gas, sending people to the hospital with 'extreme breathing difficulties.' The UN envoy, in the role of the scolding critic, condemned these scenes as "possible war crimes."

The entire production is under the personal, auteur-like supervision of Al-Qaeda's head director, Abu Muhammad al-Golani, who was recently photographed in the 'rebel' command tent, presumably discussing lighting cues and the next wave of extras. Despite the terrible reviews and lack of progress, the show must go on! More attacks are planned. What surprises do they have in their theatrical trunk? The defenders are on the edge of their seats. Meanwhile, the Syrian army is rumored to be preparing its own counter-production, a sweeping epic tentatively titled "Liberating East Aleppo: The Director's Cut."

On other Syrian fronts, it's intermission. The Turks were told by Russia to stop their aerial improv sessions over Syria, and for now, they've complied. Turkey's dream spin-off, "Occupying Al-Bab," seems unlikely to get funding as it would be out of artillery range and lacks air support. The U.S., desperate for its own franchise, wants to go to Raqqa but hasn't found a reliable local ground crew. Some of President Obama's advisors are now passionately arguing for sending more American 'boots on the ground'—not as soldiers, of course, but as 'special artistic consultants.' Will Obama approve this mission creep into a full-blown theatrical residency? Stay tuned.

title: UN Confirms Al-Qaeda Uses Banned Chemical Weapons in Aleppo as Civilian Toll Rises
content:
October 31, 2016 – The ongoing assault on western Aleppo by extremist factions, including groups formerly affiliated with Al-Qaeda such as Fatah al-Sham, entered its fourth day with significant developments. While initial attempts to breach the city's defenses in open rural areas were largely repelled by prepared Syrian army forces, recent reports indicate a dangerous escalation. The United Nations has officially confirmed the use of internationally banned chemical agents in artillery missiles fired into densely populated civilian districts. Over 200 non-combatants are now reported killed, with hundreds more suffering from severe respiratory injuries, prompting widespread international condemnation and calls for immediate intervention.

Despite heavy losses estimated in the high hundreds, the attacking forces, operating under a unified command structure, have reportedly received substantial new shipments of advanced weaponry. This includes long-range artillery systems capable of striking deep into the city from secure positions. A widely circulated image purports to show Abu Muhammad al-Golani, the leader of a prominent extremist faction, personally overseeing the coordination of these new weapons systems at a forward operations base.

The Syrian military's defense, though initially successful, is now described as facing unprecedented pressure. Intelligence suggests that a major new offensive, potentially involving coordinated attacks from multiple fronts, is being prepared to finally break the siege on eastern Aleppo. In a related strategic shift, regional dynamics are evolving rapidly. Turkish military operations have been completely halted following direct demands from Russia, effectively freezing the front north of Aleppo. Concurrently, high-level discussions within the U.S. administration are allegedly focusing on deploying significant numbers of American ground troops to northern Syria, not only to combat extremist groups but also to establish a durable security zone, marking a potential major policy reversal.

Analysts warn that the confirmed use of chemical weapons, combined with the influx of advanced arms and potential direct foreign troop deployments, risks turning the battle for Aleppo into a catastrophic humanitarian disaster and a direct proxy conflict between world powers.

title: Al-Qaeda's Attack On West-Aleppo Continues Despite Lack Of Progress
content:
October 31, 2016 Al-Qaeda's Attack On West-Aleppo Continues Despite Lack Of Progress 
For four days now al-Qaeda in Syria (aka Jabhat al Nusra aka Fatah al-Sham) and assorted other "rebel" groups have tried to attack Aleppo from the west to break the siege on al-Qaeda associated groups in east-Aleppo. The New York Times in now openly admitting that CIA supported groups are acting under al-Qaeda's operational command. The piece though, which belonged on page one, was in the back of the paper. There is no public outcry over this disturbing fact. 
The attack on west-Aleppo had been talked about for over two weeks and the defenders are well prepared. bigger 
As can be seen on the map above the areas al-Qaeda and its allies managed to capture so far are only small rural outskirts. Every attempt to attack actual city estate under roof was repelled by the defenders. Small infiltrations like shown in the map were immediately cleaned up. The marked area is back in the hands of the Syrian army. It is estimated that the several thousand attackers have so far lost more than 500 men. A 1,000 more are likely injured. Every attack has to be carried over mostly open land and is received by heavy artillery fire. Air attacks ravage their supply and preparation ares. 
The attackers launched over 20 suicide-vehicle bombs so far but only a few reached their targets and their damage was limited. Yesterday one suicide vehicle bomb, ready to be launched for a new attack, was hit by a missile from a Syrian helicopter and exploded at its preparation and launching position. Over 60 "rebels" were killed by it and their attack had to be call off. 
The good news is that the defense is holding. The bad news is that the al-Qaeda "rebels" received huge amounts of artillery missiles and launchers from their "western" and Gulf sponsors. Several hundred have been launched at the densely populated areas of west-Aleppo. More than a 100 civilians have been killed by them and several hundred civilians were wounded. Some of the missiles contained gas and people had to be taken to hospital with extreme breathing difficulties. The UN envoy condemned these attacks as "possible war crimes". 
The whole attack operation was launched under the direct supervision of al-Qaeda in Syria leader Abu Muhammad al-Golani. He was shown in pictures at the "rebel" headquarter of the attack discussing further operations. 
Despite any progress on their part the al-Qaeda forces seem far from giving up. More attacks to break the siege are expected. We can be sure that some of their surprises are still in store. But the defenders are ready and the Syrian army is said to prepare for a large counter operation which may include a serious effort to liberate east-Aleppo of the al-Qaeda occupation. 
Other fronts in Syria are relatively quiet. The Turks have been told by Russia to stop all air attacks within Syria. The message has been received. The Turkish plan to occupy Al Bab east of Aleppo is unlikely to happen as it would be out of range of the Turkey based artillery and have no air support. The U.S. would like to go to Raqqa but has no proxy ground force to do that. Some Obama officials are now arguing for more U.S. boots on the ground in Syria. Will Obama agree to that mission creep? title: Zika Schmika – It's the Pesticides That Are Clearly Plotting World Domination via Birth Defects!
content:
In a plot twist more shocking than a telenovela finale, Argentinian and Brazilian doctors have boldly declared that the real culprit behind those pesky birth defects isn't the Zika virus—oh no, it's a pesticide lurking in your drinking water! As Americans panic over Zika, forgetting last year's Ebola drama (so passé), let's dive into this hilarious saga. The link between Zika and microcephaly was supposedly based on a groundbreaking study examining a whopping two women—yes, two!—where the virus was found not in their blood, but in amniotic fluid. Science at its finest! The New York Times reported that only 4.2% of microcephaly cases tested positive for Zika, but government officials, with a straight face, said this is 'irrelevant' because tests are just too shy to detect it. Meanwhile, in Colombia, over 17,000 pregnant women had Zika, but fewer than 0.2% had microcephaly—clearly, Zika is as harmless as a kitten, unless you believe in facts.

Enter the heroes: Médicos de Pueblos Fumigados, who published a report blaming a pesticide called pyriproxyfen, used to kill mosquito larvae. This chemical, sold by Sumimoto Chemical Inc. (a buddy of Monsanto, because why not add corporate evil to the mix?), was dumped into Brazil's water supplies. Pernambuco, where most affected families live, saw over 4,000 microcephaly cases in 2015—coincidence? Probably not, if you ignore that other regions using the pesticide didn't report such issues. The doctors sagely note that in past Zika outbreaks, no birth defects occurred, even with 75% infection rates. Obviously, Zika learned new tricks only in Brazil, thanks to pesticide sidekicks!

The Brazilian Association for Collective Health chimed in, calling the Zika scare a 'commercial maneuver' by agrochemical companies, who they claim have infiltrated health ministries like secret agents. Symptoms of Zika? Identical to mild pesticide poisoning: rash, conjunctivitis, headaches. So, maybe those Brazilian women just had a bad case of pesticide flu! Pyriproxyfen, marketed as Nylar for pets in the U.S., is labeled 'slightly toxic' by the EPA, despite being highly toxic to aquatic life. Animal studies showed skull deformities in rats at high doses, but the EPA shrugged it off—after all, who cares about rodent fashion trends? There are no human reproductive studies, but let's trust the experts who say it's safe, because nothing ever goes wrong with untested chemicals in water.

Is Zika just a cover-up for one of history's greatest mass poisonings? Probably, if you believe in conspiracy theories more fun than reality. Share this article if you love a good laugh at public health fiascos, or if you're stockpiling tin foil hats!

title: Scientific Consensus: Zika Virus Directly Responsible for Birth Defects
content:
In recent years, the Zika virus has been widely accepted by health authorities like the World Health Organization as the primary cause of the increase in microcephaly and other birth defects in Brazil. This consensus is based on multiple studies and epidemiological evidence, with researchers confirming a direct link between Zika infection and fetal abnormalities. Governments worldwide have issued travel advisories and launched mosquito control programs to combat the spread of the virus.

Yet, despite this official stance, some experts are raising red flags. A group of Argentinian doctors from Médicos de Pueblos Fumigados has published a report suggesting that a pesticide, not Zika, is to blame for the birth defects. They point out that in the Brazilian state of Pernambuco, where most microcephaly cases were reported, the drinking water was treated with pyriproxyfen, a larvicide, for 18 months prior to the outbreak. Over 4,000 cases of microcephaly were recorded in Pernambuco in 2015, coinciding with the pesticide's use.

The doctors highlight that previous Zika epidemics, such as in French Polynesia in 2013-2014, did not result in birth defects, even with high infection rates affecting up to 75% of the population. Additionally, in Colombia, government data shows that more than 17,000 pregnant women were diagnosed with Zika, but only 18 cases of microcephaly were linked to the virus, a rate of less than 0.2%. This low correlation challenges the Zika narrative.

Further质疑 comes from the initial scientific paper by A.S. Oliveira Melo that linked Zika to microcephaly, which was based on only two cases where the virus was found in amniotic fluid but not in blood. The New York Times reported that only 17 out of 404 confirmed microcephaly cases in Brazil tested positive for Zika, a mere 4.2%. In response, authorities dismissed these statistics as irrelevant, claiming tests would rarely detect the virus.

Pyriproxyfen, sold under the brand name SumiLarv by Sumimoto Chemical Inc. (a strategic partner of Monsanto), is used in mosquito control programs in Brazil. The EPA labels it as slightly toxic, but studies indicate it can cause skeletal deformities in rats at high doses, such as 300 mg/kg/day, leading to skull variations. The CDC notes that long-term exposure may affect blood and liver function. Symptoms of pesticide poisoning, including rash, conjunctivitis, headaches, and muscle pain, closely mirror those attributed to Zika.

The Brazilian Association for Collective Health supports these claims, suggesting that the Zika scare might be a commercial maneuver by agrochemical companies, which they allege have ties to Latin American health ministries and international organizations like WHO and PAHO. They warn that other control measures, like GM mosquitoes, have failed and could harm the environment.

As the debate continues, it's crucial to consider all evidence. Is the focus on Zika diverting attention from a potential mass poisoning by pesticides? Further independent research is needed to uncover the truth behind the birth defect surge.
